full_text: (Photo by Alika Jenner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts , a survey of fans across the NFL. Each week, we send out questions to the most plugged-in Kansas City Chiefs fans. You can see all of the recent survey results here . And be sure to check out FanDuel Sportsbook , the official sportsbook partner of SB Nation. Chiefs fans’ confidence What a difference a few weeks makes. Last month, we ran the same poll, and 92% of Chiefs fans were confident the franchise was heading in the right direction. That was before back-to-back losses, one in the closing seconds to a division rival after a fourth-quarter collapse by all three phases. It was also back when Kenneth Walker III looked completely otherworldly, not just really, really, really good. It also doesn’t help that the Chiefs are coming off one of the worst statistical pass-rushing performances in recent memory. With the trade deadline around the corner, there is a feeling amongst some Chiefs fans that Kansas City needs to make a big move to keep from wasting a second straight year of quarterback Patrick Mahomes’ prime. So this could also be where the low confidence in the direction of the franchise. There is also the fringe group of fans whose faith in Andy Reid is starting to waver as well, as some of his past game management warts are starting to creep back up again on a roster that is not talented enough to cover up the blemishes. Whatever the reason is, there is only one way to raise confidence, and that’s by winning football games. They have a chance to start rebuilding the fans’ faith in them this week against the New York Jets . Where to worry It’s a little surprising to me that Chiefs Kingdom voted that 46% of you believe that Kansas City’s offense is their most worrisome unit right now. Especially coming off a game where the offense moved the ball relatively well against a really good defense. Now, obviously, late-game coaching decisions and the ability to punch the ball into the end zone on the final play into the decision, but given the special teams unit’s gaffes in recent weeks, I was sure that they would be selected as the unit causing the most hand-wringing. What this tells me is that Chiefs fans are worried that the offense’s issues are deeper and harder to fix than getting a new return man or kicker. Chiefs Kingdom is worried that our offensive tackles are subpar and we are in desperate need of more top-end talent at the wide receiver position. These things are harder to fix in season, and your votes reflect that. Click here to see other recent survey results.

title: 5 Qs, 5 As: Washington fans ‘hate’ the name Commanders
summary: The Washington football team (not to be confused with the Washington Football Team) is on their fifth season of being named the Commanders. And it sounds as though fans of the team are no bigger fans of “Commanders” today than they were in 2022. In fact, the longer they go into the name change, the […]
full_text: The Washington football team (not to be confused with the Washington Football Team) is on their fifth season of being named the Commanders. And it sounds as though fans of the team are no bigger fans of “Commanders” today than they were in 2022. In fact, the longer they go into the name change, the more they might want to change it again. It’s hard for me to imagine or accept that there is a team in the NFL named the “Commanders”, which still feels like a made-up name for a fictional pro football league in a Keanu Reeves or Kevin Costner movie. Even so, this is the name that they’re stuck with today, and it is the team that the Los Angeles Rams will face on Sunday in a critical moment for both franchises: If the Rams lose, all hell could break loose before the trade deadline Tuesday. If the Commanders lose, head coach Dan Quinn may not be associated with the “football team” by Monday . Washington is 2-4-1 and seeking their second win in a row since the return of quarterback Jayden Daniels. To get to know them — and their Football Team Fans — better, I sent five questions to Andrew Y at Hogs Haven. He sent me back five answers. Go…Team. Q: The Commanders don’t have a player in the top-30 for rushing yards or the top-60 for receiving yards. I feel like that would be very disappointing for fans, to not have one skill player so far this season who you can at least look forward to watching, win or lose. But those are stats, not necessarily reality. Who is the one healthy skill player on the team who Washington fans can look forward to watching each week? A: I think the player most Commanders fans would point to is rookie WR and 3rd-round pick Antonio Williams. He’s shown tremendous route-running nuance and short-area quickness to get open in the middle field and has been a consistent target getter, with 23 catches for 259 yards so far this season. Those simple stats don’t rely do credit to his ability though, as he’s generated a 96.7 passer rating when targeted and is PFF’s second-highest graded rookie receiver. Dan Quinn made clear that with the loss of Terry McLaurin, he expects Antonio Williams’ role to increase the most and indeed Williams led all receivers in snaps and routes last week against the Eagles. Q: Five years in, how is the name “Commanders” sitting with fans? Do you ever long for the days of Football Team again? A: Honestly, I think most fans hate the name Commanders. It’s the last stinky gift given to us by former owner Dan Snyder that the new leadership hasn’t been able to reverse. The names that seemed most popular with fans (and with me) were Red Wolves (a nod to the old name, but with a cool animal attached) or Warthogs (which has alliteration with Washington and could be shortened to ‘Hogs to reference the famous Hogs offensive line of the glory days). There is a contingent of fans that actually liked the name Washington Football Team and many would probably still take it over Commanders, but I always suspected it was more driven by nostalgia for the old name and a feeling that if we can’t have that name, then no name is better. Washington Football Team feels to me more like having no name and certainly doesn’t lend itself to new branding. I’d rather have a new team name and branding, it just needs to be a good name and good branding. Q: It’s the end of 2026 and the beginning of 2027. No changes have been made yet. Dan Quinn is the head coach, Adam Peters is the GM, the roster is intact. If you can make one change to the Commanders team/organization to set them on the right path, what do you do? A: Unless the rest of the season plays out very differently than it has up until now, I would fire Dan Quinn and let Adam Peters lead a search to choose the next head coach. I think Adam Peters has actually done a pretty good job of rebuilding the roster and giving the team enough depth to withstand an avalanche of injuries this year. However, they often look poorly coached, with the most yards erased by penalty in the NFL, slow playcalls and players taking too much time to get into position, and regular mistakes in situational awareness and game management that lose games. However, one other change needs to be made. The biggest reason the team was able to go on that 2024 playoff run and has been unable to repeat is that our 2024 season was one of our healthiest ever, with few major injuries to core players in the regular season. That’s a major outlier, as Washington has had the most Adjusted Games Lost (AGL) due to injury in the NFL since 2009 (!) and only the Giants have been in the same tier of AGL. This year is no different, with four of the team’s highest-paid players already done for the season. To be one of the NFL’s most-injured teams over that span of time is significant and unusual in that it covers multiple front office staffs, coaching staffs, and even medical staffs. The one constant in that time has been the strength and conditioning staff, led by Chad Englehart. Englehart started as an assistant strength and conditioning coach in 2010 before being promoted to head of strength and conditioning in 2017. He’s stayed on so long because he’s extremely popular with players and rates highly in NFLPA surveys, but I’m convinced his staff are doing something that leads to Washington’s players being more injury prone, perhaps by over-training them. An outlier injury rate over 17 years can’t be simple bad luck. I would order a full external evaluation of the team’s strength & conditioning program and make major changes there. Q: Who are you happier to see fail this season: The Cowboys or the Eagles? A: It’s a delight to see both of them fail, but more so the Eagles. The Eagles have come to be seen by people around the NFL as the “class of the division” and their fans love to loudly reiterate that belief. It’s great seeing them get taken down a peg with a nightmare season most didn’t see coming. I’ve noticed there’s a bit of an age gap in how people respond to this question. Most fans over 50ish years of age hate the Cowboys more and still vividly remember “we want Dallas” chants and the heyday of the rivalry from the 80s and 90s, but I think younger fans would generally prefer to watch the Eagles flounder. Q: What’s your happiest memory of the Washington team over the last 30 years? What’s been the pinnacle of being a fan of this team since the mid 90s? A: Honestly, my happiest memory in that time period was when Dan Snyder finally sold the team. His rotten ownership had been the millstone around the team’s neck that prevented it from ever rising up and ensured it was always surrounded by negative drama. Most fans by that point knew we’d never be a serious football operation with Dan Snyder in charge, so the sale was the first real light after a long period of darkness that signalled things could finally change. I wasn’t prepared for how quickly that would happen though, because then followed the Commanders 2024 season with a dynamic rookie QB. That season blew out anything that happened under the Dan Snyder era: first time the team won 12 regular-season games since the ’91 Super Bowl team, first time the team made the NFC Championship game since the ’91 team, etc. In addition, so many of those games ended in exciting, last-minute wins that the team got the nickname “Cardiac Commanders.” That season was the pinnacle of being a fan of the team since the mid-90s. The victory over the Lions in the playoffs was the single best game, because nobody expected us to boat race the Lions and advance to the conference championship like that.

title: Aaron Donald wants to be better for Rams after missed opportunity
summary: Aaron Donald almost recovered a fumble in Week 8 against the Los Angeles Chargers, and had Donald actually recovered that ball, he may have scored a touchdown. Instead, Donald botched the recovery and he was left with nothing. If you watch Donald talk about it, underneath the laugher for this blunder, he knows he needs […]
full_text: Aaron Donald almost recovered a fumble in Week 8 against the Los Angeles Chargers, and had Donald actually recovered that ball, he may have scored a touchdown. Instead, Donald botched the recovery and he was left with nothing. "If anybody knew how hard it is at our age to go down there and get a ball." Matthew Stafford felt for Aaron Donald after he missed the mark on the fumble recovery 😭 @insidethenfl Week 8 Mic'd Up on X pic.twitter.com/vOfSbC7kj4 — NFL (@NFL) November 2, 2026 If you watch Donald talk about it, underneath the laugher for this blunder, he knows he needs to be better. He talks about the reality that if the Rams didn’t win, or if they were trailing, not recovering the ball wouldn’t have been such a laughing matter. Donald wants to be better for the Rams, and the Rams will need him and everyone to play at their best to recover from their 4-4 start. Rams’ Aaron Donald Breaks Down Viral Muffed Fumble Opportunity (sports.yahoo) “Donald explained that he may have gotten a bit too excited about the chances of scoring his first-ever defensive touchdown, which led to his missing out completely on the fumble recovery. “Boom. I seen the ball. First thing came to my head. ‘Touchdown. I’m going to get this ball.’ I should have slowed down, but I felt people behind me like I want to get hit in my back. That’s going to hurt. So, I tried to go full speed and scoop it. The ball was going I thought the ball was going to bounce this way, but it bounced that way. And it just looked all damn silly,” Donald said. “ Aaron Donald gets brutally honest about Rams return (nypost) “The 35-year-old three-time Defensive Player of the Year made a candid admission about his return to The Sporting Tribune’s Eric Lambkins II. “No, it’s not what I expected, but we here,” Donald said of his return. He then added, “And I’m going to enjoy it though, you know. I’m enjoying the process. I’m enjoying myself week in and week out getting better. I’m enjoying being out there with the guys.” “Ain’t what I expected, but I’m enjoying it,” he added. Donald also spoke about getting Myles Garrett back healthy in Los Angeles’ upcoming game against the Washington Commanders, as Garrett has been sidelined since the Rams’ Week 1 game.“ Myles Garrett expected to play vs. Commanders (ramswire) “The returns of Garrett and Ferguson will both be huge for the Rams, who have missed them over the last month-plus. Josaiah Stewart will now take on a more limited role in the pass-rush rotation, while Ferguson steps in immediately and becomes the Rams’ top pass-catching tight end. With Davante Adams out, the Rams badly need another receiving threat, and Ferguson provides just that. Garrett, meanwhile, is the reigning Defensive Player of the Year and the record-holder for the most sacks in a season (23).“ NFL predictions: Washington Commanders vs Los Angeles Rams (sports.yahoo) “Brown is a former playoff hero with the Commanders who lit up the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Detroit Lions during 2025’s playoff run, before wilting with 42 yards in the NFC Title Game against the Philadelphia Eagles. Brown has played in seven games this season and has contributed, albiet at a reduced rate, with nine receptions for 94 yards and no touchdowns. He has been dealing with a calf injury. Burks has been ramping up his production this season with 12 catches for 233 yards and two touchdowns, including 81 yards against the Eagles on November 1. He is dealing with a left foot injury.“ Myles Garrett Set to Make Return vs. Commanders, But What Should Rams Expect? (si.com) “The Rams traded for Garrett in what was their biggest acquisition of the offseason . However, shortly into training camp, Garrett began missing practices with what was described as knee soreness and then was placed on injured reserve that week as he underwent arthroscopic surgery. “There were just things I was dealing with mechanically that only continued to worsen as I played more throughout that game,” said Garrett on Friday. “It was rough and I was trying to avoid it, but you learn and you grow. Now it’s just a lesson that I had to learn from and I took the necessary steps to come back.” With Jaylen Watson heading on injured reserve earlier this week, the Rams won’t get a look at what their defense could have been with Garrett, Watson, Trent McDuffie, and Aaron Donald. However, the Rams will get a look at what their defense can do with Donald and Garrett on the field together for the first time.“ Myles Garrett’s Expected Return Gives Los Angeles Rams a Pass-Rush Boost (athlonsports) “Locked On Rams Squad Show host Gavin Carlson said Garrett can help compensate for Watson’s absence by shortening the time Daniels has to diagnose coverage. Carlson’s central point was not that one pass rusher erases the loss of a productive cornerback; it is that Garrett can force quicker decisions, creating more manageable coverage situations for the defensive backs who remain.” Rams safety Quentin Lake apologizes to Justin Herbert for ‘deli meat’ comment, even though he has a point (sports.yahoo) “According to The Los Angeles Times, Lake sent an apology to Herbert over text message, but had not heard back. “I don’t know if he read it,” Lake said. “He probably says, ‘I don’t care about it anymore. I’m not trying to see this. It doesn’t matter. You said what you said.’ But at the same time I … felt like it was right for me to at least say, ‘Hey, man, I didn’t mean it in any disrespectful way.'” Come on, Justin: He meant you were throwing deli meat in the most respectful way imaginable!“ Rams listed Matthew Stafford with elbow injury because reporters asked about ice on it (sports.yahoo) “Really, it’s because you guys asked me about it earlier in the week,” McVay told reporters on Friday regarding the decision to disclose an elbow injury for Stafford. “It’s more semantical than anything else. It’s normal, like what he told you guys, but because you guys asked me about him having ice on his elbow. . . . He’s been full, hasn’t missed any sort of reps so normal management stuff that he’s been doing over the last few years.” It conjures memories of the Patriots’ one-time habit of listing former quarterback Tom Brady as “probable” with a “right shoulder” injury. That all started because he had ice on his shoulder in the locker room, reporters inquired, and the team decided to just put him on the injury report every week.“ Los Angeles Rams Announce Bad News About Former Top Draft Pick (heavy.com) “Grant Stuard will be limited with his hamstring. He’ll be questionable for the game. Jordan Whittington will be limited with his back. He’ll be questionable for the game. We’ll end up putting Jaylen Watson on IR, but he’s listed as out on this injury report. Joe Cardona will be doubtful. Trent McDuffie , Colby Parkinson, and Kam Curl , they’ll be listed as questionable for the game. Trent will be a DNP. Everybody else has no injury designation.” Rams & Commanders set for a crucial NFC showdown in Week 9 | Game Preview (therams.com) “Key contributors continue to peel off to the injured list, sapping what should be some nice momentum for the Rams. When you think back to how this roster was constructed, it’s deflating to come to grips with the fact that we’ll see zero snaps of Trent McDuffie , Jaylen Watson , Myles Garrett , and Aaron Donald playing football together in 2026. “I think you’ll miss the production, the toughness, some of the different things that we’re able to do with him,” Sean McVay remarked this week as Watson accepted season-ending surgery on his twice-injured shoulder. “A couple of weeks ago, he’s cramping at the Raiders game and he says when he’s getting an IV, ‘Give me half a bag. I need to get back out there.’ He’s been awesome. He’s been playing through some different stuff, but he’s been really productive, and it’s unfortunate that that happened.” Comment of the day: Feed post of the day:

full_text: In pursuit of a third consecutive win, the Los Angeles Rams travel cross-country to take on the Washington Commanders. Kickoff is set for 10 a.m. PST from Northwest Stadium in Landover, Maryland. The nation’s capitol eleven currently stands at 2-4-1 and are coming off a 27-10 win over the Philadelphia Eagles. Washington’s offense is ranked in the bottom third of NFL teams for the season, but have trended upward slightly over the last three games with the return from injury of quarterback Jayden Daniels. The Rams have had their struggles defending athletic quarterbacks who can extend drives with their running ability and Daniels is adept at that. While injuries have detoured his and the team’s success since his Rookie of the Year performance in 2024, he is still dangerous and has yet to throw an interception in 2026. Daniels does good work spreading out the receiving targets, veteran Stefon Diggs and rookie Antonio Williams being the primaries. Both should get a lot of work Sunday, secondary receivers Dyami Brown (calf) and Treylon Burks (foot) have been ruled out of the game with injury. The Commanders run game has struggled, Rachaad White and Jacory McCrosky-Merritt have combined for a paltry 439 yards. The big news for the Rams is the expected return of edge Myles Garrett off the Injured Reserve List. It will be his first action since Week 1. Tight end Terrance Ferguson was also anticipated to play after missing five weeks, but has been downgraded to out for the game. Here’s how to follow the game! Location: Northwest Stadium in Landover, Maryland Date: Sunday, November 8 Time: 10:00 a.m. PST Watch on TV Nationally: FOX Play-By-Play: Chris Myers Color Analyst: Mark Schlereth Sideline Reporter: Jen Hale Streaming In past seasons, a live stream was available on the following platforms if the game is available on TV in the local market. title: What is San Francisco 49ers’ offense missing without Mike Evans in Week 9 against the Las Vegas Raiders?
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders face a tough test in Week 9, squaring off against the NFC-leading San Francisco 49ers. This will be an opportunity for the Raiders to announce themselves as a legitimate playoff contender heading into the second half of the season, but that won’t come easy. To preview the game, Silver and Black […]
full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders face a tough test in Week 9 , squaring off against the NFC-leading San Francisco 49ers . This will be an opportunity for the Raiders to announce themselves as a legitimate playoff contender heading into the second half of the season, but that won’t come easy. To preview the game, Silver and Black Pride reached out to our friends at Niners Nation, and Kyle Posey was kind enough to answer a few questions about the 49ers for Raider Nation. Q: With the 49ers, we have to start with injuries. Granted, the team had its bye last week to heal up. So, what’s the status of San Francisco’s key players who have been banged up recently? Also, should the Raiders be worried about playing next to the ominous electrical substation? A: General manager John Lynch has already ruled out Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel for this game. It seems like their WR2, Demarcus Robinson, will return. The team will still be short-handed at wide receiver. The injury report is forever lengthy with this team. Christian McCaffrey will likely be listed as questionable, although he’s expected to play. I wouldn’t bank on seeing a heavy workload from CMC, even if it’s after a bye week. The good news is that the 49ers are getting Nick Bosa back; it appears. He’s the engine of the defense. There are a couple of role players who will have questionable designations. One is safety Marques Sigle, who started every game up until an injury in Week 4. It seems like he’s on track to return, but he may not get his spot back. Maybe the Niners put some voodoo on the substation during their bye so it can finally stop zapping this team with injuries. Q: On a related note, wide receiver Mike Evans was the 49ers’ biggest offseason addition but likely won’t play on Sunday. What is the offense missing without Evans, and who needs to step up to fill his shoes? A: Evans is everything the 49ers could have imagined, and then some. He has an explosive play rate of 29.6%. Brock Purdy probably feels like he can throw it to Evans blindfolded and still have the confidence that he’d come down with the reception. Evans has kept the offense on the field countless times on third downs. He’s averaging 17.2 yards per reception on non-red zone targets. He’s objectively been their biggest asset on offense, the same offense that’s No. 1 in most advanced statistics. There isn’t an Evans replacement on the roster, which is the problem. Not that any team would be able to replace its best player, but the Niners go from 6’5” Evans to sub-6′ Brandin Cooks and Jacob Cowing, or second-year pro Jordan Watkins. Robinson is “fine” as a WR2, but when he was the primary target in 2025, the offense still sputtered. The easy answer is George Kittle and Christian McCaffrey need to step up, but this could be a game where Watkins sees the most targets he has all season. Q: While everyone knows about Christian McCaffrey at this point, McCaffrey’s rushing attempts are down from 18.3 per game in 2025 to 12.0 so far in 2026 . Presumably, that’s because of rookie running back Kaelon Black’s emergence. What can you tell us about Fernando Mendoza’s college teammate’s role in the 49ers’ offense? Is Kyle Shanahan shifting toward a two-running-back approach with McCaffrey turning 30 years old this summer? A: Black out-carried McCaffrey in Week 1, and everybody thought that’s how things would be all season. Shanahan has made it a point to reduce McCaffrey’s role after an insane workload in 2025. He’s done a good job of resisting the urge to give CMC a 25- 30-touch game. It won’t be easy to continue that without Evans, but Black could go a long way in making sure McCaffrey stays healthy. The rookie hasn’t offered much of anything in the passing game. He’s been OK as a runner. He’s a tough kid who gets yards after contact, but the big-play ability that we saw in college has been lacking. That changed last game, when Black ripped off a 30-yard run. Perhaps that’ll give him the confidence needed moving forward. I’d say Black was mildly disappointing through the first month, but improved the past two games. I’d also imagine he gets a semi-decent workload with McCaffrey nursing an injury. Q: A little more than six years after trading him to Indianapolis, DeForest Buckner came back to San Francisco via trade last week. Why was this move needed, and what do you expect to see from Buckner in his return? A: The 49ers have been decimated by injury along the defensive line. Both their starters at defensive tackle hit the injured reserve. They’ve been rotating a pass-rush first player, a rookie, and a second-year undrafted free agent at those spots for over a month. You could see last game how gassed their tackles were. Buckner is a player who rarely comes off the field. The trickle-down effect of having him in the lineup will make everybody else better because they don’t have to play in roles where they can’t shine. I think Buckner is going to look like one of the biggest deadline steals when we look back, because he’s precisely what the Niners need at defensive tackle. He’s a force as a pass rusher, and strong enough to hold his own against the run. I expect big things from Buckner. Q: Normally, putting a linebacker on Brock Bowers is a bad idea. However, Fred Warner is on a different level and might be the exception. How do you think those two match up against each other, and/or do you think 49ers defensive coordinator Raheem Morris will go with a different strategy against Bowers? A: It’s best on best. Bowers is arguably the best skill player in the NFL. He’s amazing. Warner has held the title of best linebacker all decade. But he hasn’t really been used in man-to-man situations, and I don’t think that changes here. Klint Kubiak is smart enough to move Bowers around the formation; that way, you can’t key on him. It’ll be one of the biggest challenges the 49ers have faced in some time. The Falcons had success dinking and dunking their way downfield. I know that’s not how the Raiders use Bowers, but quick passes are the way to get over on the Niners, as they go out of their way to take away the deep pass. I’d imagine it’s a 10+ target game for Bowers. How his yardage looks is another story, but he should find success against the Niners’ zone coverage. The defense has not fared well when it comes to its nickels and safeties in coverage.

title: Beating Kyle Shanahan would be quite the feather in Klint Kubiak’s cap
summary: Want to a crystal clear example of the kind of football team Klint Kubiak wants his Las Vegas Raiders to become? Eye the San Francisco 49ers very closely this Sunday. Because when Kubiak’s Raiders head to Santa Clara to go toe-to-to with Shanahan’s Niners, you’ll get a bird’s eye view a San Francisco team that […]
full_text: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Want to a crystal clear example of the kind of football team Klint Kubiak wants his Las Vegas Raiders to become? Eye the San Francisco 49ers very closely this Sunday. Because when Kubiak’s Raiders head to Santa Clara to go toe-to-to with Shanahan’s Niners, you’ll get a bird’s eye view a San Francisco team that plays complementary football and is 6-1 overall because of it. There have been fleeting moments of this for Las Vegas, however, the inability to harness consistency is a big reason why the team is 4-4 overall. Curious as to why Shanahan’s football team is one to model for Kubiak? The pair of head coaches are steeped in the game, thanks to the coaching connection between their fathers Mike Shanahan and Gary Kubiak. The Kyle and Klint dynamic goes back to 1994 when Mike was the offensive coordinator and Gary the quarterbacks coach of the 49ers Super Bowl-winning coaching staff. The elder Shanahan and Kubiak continued to be tied at the hip with the Denver Broncos. “Not a first one. Just really fortunate to grow up in that environment,” Klint Kubiak said on a first memory he had with Kyle Shanahan with their dads coaching together. “I didn’t know it at the time, but I got to be exposed to a lot of football at a young age, and I’m very grateful for that, myself and my brothers.” When Gary became the Houston Texans head coach, he gave Kyle his start as an offensive coordinator. And, in 2023, Kyle and Klint joined forces where the Kubiak was the passing game coordinator with the Shanahan dialing up the offense as head coach. Source confirms former Broncos QB coach Klint Kubiak is joining 49ers offensive staff in some capacity. Dad Gary Kubiak was a top assistant for Mike Shanahan during 49er/Bronco heydays in 90s. Now son Klint working for Kyle Shanahan (as is Kay Kubiak). #9sports — Mike Klis (@mikeklis) February 16, 2023 There’s mutual respect and trust between the two families. And with a storied history together, similarities were bound to happen. Foundationally, Shanahan’s and Kubiak’s respective offenses are deeply rooted in the same coaching tree. It’s a philosophy designed to scheme play makers open with pre-snap motions and a balanced attack that showcases a physical and productive ground game. Specializing in the outside/wide-zone run scheme, the 49ers and Raiders eat off play action and the pre-snap motions both play callers habitually use not only identify and stress coverage schemes, but get pass catchers open. Shanahan and Kubiak know to use running backs and tight ends in a variety of ways, so much so, that pass catching tailbacks and tight ends are often primary targets when the aerial attack is dialed up. As the longstanding relationship between the two is undeniable, what’s also without question is the two having their own distinct twist of the Shanahan-Kubiak offense. Klint, for example, blended modern, rhythm-based passing concepts into the time-tested zone play-action tenets the system offers. Taking into account the history between the two and the inherent competitiveness between them, beating Shanahan’s 49ers this Sunday would be quite the feather in Kubiak’s cap. Even now, there’s another branch in the Shanahan-Kubiak dynamic as Klint’s brother Klay is the 49ers offensive coordinator. 49ers offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak talks about coaching against his brother, Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak, on Sunday: "He's rooting for a good competition and a good handshake after the game." 🎥: @49ers #RaiderNation | #FTTB pic.twitter.com/9N5yNGGqHt — Vegas Sports Today (@VegasSportsTD) November 6, 2026 Like Shanahan, Kubiak won’t be alone in his endeavor to coach his team past the 49ers and get his Raiders to back-to-back wins and a 5-4 record instead of a 4-5 mark. Kubiak’s chosen defensive coordinator — Rob Leonard — and special teams coordinator — Joe DeCamillis — must hold up their ends of the bargain in order to play complementary football against a really good 49ers team coming off its bye week. San Francisco is eyeing winning it’s seventh game of the year as a proper bounce back from getting beat by the Atlanta Falcons 29-20 two Sunday’s ago. Las Vegas’ defense will have its hand full stopping Shanahan and the fact Leonard’s group is a cellar dweller statistically league-wise . Playing with much more discipline and urgency, alongside Leonard dialing up blitzes, is a must as the Raiders defense has allowed 30 or more points in the last five games. “Well, I think if you’ve worked in the NFL long enough, then that’s the reality of our business. It’s a production business,” Kubiak said of the confidence he has in Leonard. “It’s the most competitive industry that I know of, and any time that you start to feel comfortable, then you will be quickly humbled. And so, whether you’re having success or you’re working to get better, if your mindset stays the same and you continue to push and push through the hard times, you come out on the other end. So, that’s the NFL. The NFL brings adversity and makes you answer to it every day.” Offensively, Kubiak has veteran Kirk Cousins at quarterback producing 19 touchdown passes (second most int he league) to just five interceptions. Brock Bowers remains a reliable target for Cousins and is a difficult cover for cornerbacks and safeties, alike. At the league meeting, 49ers HC Kyle Shanahan said #Raiders HC Klint Kubiak is an "asset" to any player he has worked with. "Anybody who has been coached by Klint truly appreciates the type of person he is." — Ryan McFadden (@ryanmcfadden_) March 30, 2026 Cousins speaks highly of the 49ers defense led by Raheem Morris, a defensive coach that left an impression on the Raiders quarterback during their time together with the Washington Commanders. “It’s a great group. They’re well coached. Fred Warner is one of the best linebackers in the league. (Nick) Bosa, Buck (DeForest Buckner), several of these guys are some of the best D-linemen in the league, and I think the secondary is also a very good group,” Cousins said about Morris’ 49ers defense. “They’ve made a lot of plays, so it’s all three levels. You see the safeties really play hard, play fast. They’ll strike you. “So, it’s a defense that played really well last year, playing really well this year. I feel like I’ve seen a lot of these same players and even somewhat the same scheme going back to when Kyle [Shanahan] first got there, and they’ve got a lot of continuity, and it shows in the tape.”

title: Raiders Mailbag: Should Las Vegas consider trading Tre Tucker?
summary: The Week 9 matchup against the San Francisco 49ers marks the halfway point of the Las Vegas Raiders’ 2026 season, and the NFL trade deadline is coming up on Tuesday. So, we have a lot to go over for this week’s mailbag. Let’s get to it! A: It depends on how they feel about re-signing […]
full_text: (Photo by Candice Ward/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Week 9 matchup against the San Francisco 49ers marks the halfway point of the Las Vegas Raiders’ 2026 season, and the NFL trade deadline is coming up on Tuesday. So, we have a lot to go over for this week’s mailbag. Let’s get to it! A: It depends on how they feel about re-signing Tre Tucker in the offseason. If John Spytek and Co. don’t want to prioritize Tucker, then it would make sense to get something for him, especially for a Top 100 pick. However, the Raiders are still in the hunt, so I don’t think they’re going to be looking to move on from starters at the deadline. As far as re-signing Tucker goes, I don’t think Jalen Nailor’s contract impacts that much. Tucker has already out-produced Nailor, with almost double the amount of yards ( 2,040 to 1,179 ) and catches (152 to 81) and has more touchdowns (14 to 12) despite being in the NFL for one fewer season. Nailor is making less than $12 million per year (ranks 40th among WRs, per Over The Cap ), and I’d bet Tucker gets something similar to Jakobi Meyer’s contract with the Jaguars ($20 million per year, 27th among WRs ). Also, it’s not ideal, but the Raiders can get out of Nailor’s contract if that becomes an issue in the offseason. Per OTC , they’d save $5.5 million and take on about $9.4 million in dead cap with a post-June 1 cut, and it’s about a 50/50 split with $7.4 million in savings via a pre-June 1 trade, and a little more than $12 million in savings with a post-June 1 trade. Again, not an ideal situation, but there are options available. Personally, I feel like the need for a ‘WR1’ is kind of diminishing by the week. The offense and passing game are functioning pretty well with Brock Bowers as the top option, while the team is struggling to find answers at guard and defensive tackle. As long as Bowers is around, I wouldn’t mind rolling with a collection of cheaper ‘WR2s’ like Tucker and allocating more resources to the trenches. However, then the issue becomes: When and how much does Bowers want to get paid? He’s going to be eligible for a contract extension in the offseason and will reset the tight end market whenever he gets his second contract. Plus, the offense’s current ‘WR1’ will probably look to get ‘WR1’ money from the Raiders, which is in the $30-plus million per year range. Q: Might there be any indication on how the Raiders will handle the trade deadline? Or do they have good poker faces? A: Coincidentally, my power rankings roundup column had some trade deadline talk in it, where ESPN dove into the best in-season trade the Raiders have ever had (DB Mike Haynes in 1983). I was trying to think of the second-best in-season acquisition the franchise has made at the deadline, and had a hard time coming up with one. The reason I bring this up is that, historically, the Raiders don’t make many moves at the deadline, at least not as a ‘buyer’. Considering that win or lose, they’ll still be in the playoff hunt after this weekend, I have a hard time seeing Kirk Cousins getting traded. On top of that, the only significant trade rumor coming out of Las Vegas right now is that Maxx Crosby is not on the market. So, maybe a smaller deal like Powers-Johnson getting traded happens, but anything else would be a surprise at this point. I get the feeling Spytek and Klint Kubiak are content to roll with the roster as is for the rest of the season and then address the needs in the offseason. A: Again, I don’t think we’ll see any splash trades coming out of Vegas in the next few days. But to answer the question: Maxx Crosby, Kirk Cousins, Tucker (third-fourth fringe), Kolton Miller (third-fourth fringe), and Ashton Jeanty. Crosby would have to be for a haul, and it sounds like the organization is trying to make it known that he isn’t going anywhere. I touched on this in more detail last week ; I’d hold onto Cousins and Miller to help support Fernando Mendoza. And I’ll save y’all some time rather than rehash my Tucker and Jeanty takes. The running back will come up again later. Q: Under Rob Leonard at defensive coordinator, Eric Stokes doesn’t look as good as he did last year. At what point do they let all 3 young CBs play both CB spots? Did the league catch on to Rob Leonard’s scheme, or why does the defense look so bad compared to the first 3 weeks? A: The problem is that Darien Porter and Hezekiah Masses are both inconsistent right now, and Jermod McCoy’s tape is pretty ugly on the limited snaps he’s played this season. So, while Stokes has regressed, he’s still probably the most reliable corner on the roster. As long as the Raiders are in the playoff mix, I don’t think the coaching staff pivots to the full-on youth movement. But once they fall out of contention, then we could see Porter, Masses and McCoy get more opportunities. As for Leonard’s scheme, opposing offenses have definitely been picking on his tendacies in the last several weeks. The first two games had a lot of mystery about what he was going to run, making it difficult for the Dolphins and Chargers to put a typical game plan together. Also, we now know those are two of the worst teams in the league. Even the Saints started to figure out Leonard, putting up 27 points in three quarters before turning the ball over on every possession in the fourth. New Orleans still racked up 381 yards, and that was our first sign that the book was out on the Raiders’ defense. The Chiefs were the first team to really highlight this; the Raiders can’t stop the run consistently against 12 and 13 personnel. I dive into that in more detail when talking about the defensive tackles. I think part of it is a talent issue to cut Leonard some slack. Ultimately, with the way it’s currently constructed from scheme and personnel perspectives, this is a very turnover-reliant defense. That’s hard to sustain because it requires the other team/offense to make mistakes. Q: Why are the Raiders struggling to find a NT for their 3-4? Do they not have to correct players on the roster? Seems like they had numerous opportunities to grab one in the draft or through a trade. Yet they shuffle through players who don’t seem to fit a true NT but are serviceable. Do they not hold NT an important position? Seems very neglectful by Spytek if your base is 3-4. A: They didn’t prioritize the position at all in the offseason. The starting nose tackle right now is Foley Fatukasi, who was signed after the first preseason game. As you mentioned, there were plenty of opportunities to address it in the offseason. This draft class had several good nose tackles, but Spytek went in a different direction every time. I think that came down to two factors. One being that the front office wasn’t going to be able to fill every need in one offseason. Think about how many starting spots were up for grabs or were questionable heading into training camp. The other factor is that the 3-4 discussion was kind of a fallacy, where Rob Leonard ideally runs a variety of fronts. In the first few games of the season, the Raiders were in more even fronts out of nickel personnel. Then, teams started to realize the defense struggles to stop 12 and 13 personnel. Leonard likes to counter those looks by putting an off-ball linebacker (typically Quay Walker) on the line of scrimmage at edge to get into an odd front. That’s where not having a good nose tackle really started to show up because teams like the Chiefs, Bills and Rams just stayed in 12 and 13 personnel, forcing the Raiders to play fronts that they aren’t adequately equipped to play. So, I think it was a combination of negligence from Spytek and the defense not functioning the way Leonard envisioned in the offseason. Granted, you could argue that the former is the cause of the latter. It’s certainly time for Spytek to place a bigger priority on the defensive tackle position as a whole than he has in the past. Lions win easily 38-20. leightonwilliams517 is focused on time of possession, and I agree; keeping the other team’s offense off the field is a good start. Alrighty so, I’m looking at TOP (time of possession) as the biggest factor of all – and also the zone coverage is letting the other WRs to get open rather easily. It’s true there’s a risk either way (no matter what coverage is utilized) as these are rookie CBs-but at least attempt to disrupt the timing of the routes to allow the pass rush to get home. USMCFinPhreak wanted to pick the Dolphins; they really, really did. Could be … Might be …Will be ugly. 30-10 Detroit. phinette believes the Lions will remind us this team isn’t quite ready to compete with the big boys yet. Lions offense will dominate. This one could get ugly early. Lions 35-13 CluelessNFLfan doesn’t see a blowout, just an offense that the Phins just can’t keep up with. Detroit offense puts up 31 points and our offense can’t keep up with that. Kitties win 31-24. DolphinsKings1 has Malik in a total collapse as the Lions destroy the Phins. 48 Lions 14 Dolphins Malik 4 Ints 2 Fumbles pulled in 4th Quarter. Ollie gets 90 on 24 carries and a TD. Goff 3 TD’s St. Brown 3 TD’s 2 pick sixes This one won’t be close at all. I want the Willis experiment to end. He is not it. Move on. If you can get a trade go for it. Or ride McCord and start evaluating. JUK has the Phins offense looking better but with similar results. I doubt we win this but I could see a decent day for the offense. I’ll say 34-24 lions It seems as if the overwhelming belief is that our Dolphins have zero chance against the Lions tomorrow. That’s probably correct, but I hope it’s one of those days when the humidity just destroys the team that practices in a nice, cool environment. summary: The Miami Dolphins are heading into their Week 9 game against the Detroit Lions surprisingly healthy for a mid-season game. full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - SEPTEMBER 13: Kadyn Proctor #74 of the Miami Dolphins leaves the field after warmups against the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. The Raiders defeated the Dolphins 27-13. (Photo by Candice Ward/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Miami Dolphins are heading into their Week 9 game against the Detroit Lions surprisingly healthy for a mid-season game. The Dolphins listed only three players on their final injury report on Friday, and all three were questionable at worst. Miami will likely have its entire roster available for the game. The Lions, meanwhile, ruled out five players, all starters. for the game. They also had three players listed as questionable. Kadyn Proctor returns Rookie guard Kadyn Proctor cleared concussion protocol after missing last week’s game against the New England Patriots. Proctor’s return to the lineup returns the Dolphins to their original starting lineup with left tackle Patrick Paul, left guard Proctor, center Aaron Brewer, right guard Jonah Savaiinaea, and right tackle Austin Jackson. On Friday, The Phinsider’s Marek Brave wrote, “ In [Proctor’s] absence , Miami’s offensive line struggled against a stout Patriots front — allowing 5 sacks and managing just 74 yards rushing on 20 attempts (just 3.7 yards per carry).“ Getting Proctor back into the lineup should assist the Dolphins as they face the ninth-ranked rush defense in the league on Sunday. Malik Willis downplays groin injury Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis, who was a full participant all week in practice, has been dealing with a groin injury for the last couple of week. He was asked this week if the injury led to a reluctance to run last week against the Patriots and he was pretty straight forward that they were not connected. “I think that’s just how the game played out. I’m not sure that had anything to do with it really,” he stated. Willis continued to be listed on the injury report this week with the injury, but was not given a game-day status, indicating he will be starting. Lions without several starters The Lions have not been as lucky with their injuries. Linebacker Jack Campbell, who sustained a serious neck injury early in last week’s game against the Minnesota Vikings, was obviously going to be ruled out of the game. Several other players were also given the “out” designation. Safety Kerby Joseph continues to work his way back from the physically unable to perform list with a knee injury. According to Pride of Detroit’s Erik Schlitt, the Lions plan on ramping up Joseph’s workload next week . He has a little over a week remaining on his practice window before the team has to move him to the 53-man roster or leave him on the PUP for the remainder of the year. Center Cade Mays has an ankle injury and the Lions have been preparing for him to be out this weekend. Juice Scruggs will start in his place. Cornerback D.J. Reed has a hip injury and has not been able to practice all week. Edge rusher DJ Wonnum has a concussion and is working his way through the protocols. Including Joseph, who will move into the starting lineup once he is activated off the PUP, all five players are starters for the Lions. Dolphins running backs questionable behind Ollie Gordon II The biggest injury concerns for the Dolphins heading into this weekend’s game may be at running back depth. While Ollie Gordon II, elevated to the starting role after De’Von Achane’s season-ending injury early this year, will see most snaps, both Jaylen Wright and Kaytron Allen are questionable for the game. While they will likely both be available, Miami’s depth may be fairly shallow if anything aggravates the quadriceps injuries nagging both players. Wright did not practice on Wednesday before being limited on both Thursday and Friday; Allen was limited for the first two days before being a full participant on Friday. Miami also listed edge rusher Malik Herring as questionable with a neck injury. He was limited in practice all week. title: Miami Dolphins offensive line review: Tracking the guards in Week 8
summary: Despite a glorious halftime lead and a legitimate chance to pull off a second consecutive win against a divisional opponent, the Dolphins faltered against the Patriots last Sunday. Still, we probably learn more from losses than wins, and this remains a season focused on learning and development. That is especially true along the offensive line, […]
full_text: Despite a glorious halftime lead and a legitimate chance to pull off a second consecutive win against a divisional opponent, the Dolphins faltered against the Patriots last Sunday. Still, we probably learn more from losses than wins, and this remains a season focused on learning and development. That is especially true along the offensive line, where rookie left guard Kadyn Proctor and second-year right guard Jonah Savaiinaea are important pieces of the team’s future. How are they performing this season? Each week, we take a closer look at the guards and what is being said about their most recent performance. Kadyn Proctor Game Snap Counts Penalties PFF Overall Grade PFF Run Blocking PFF Pass Protection 9/13, @ Raiders 59 (100%) 1 71.2 79.0 63.4 9/20, @ 49ers 56 (100%) 2 62.0 72.4 39.1 9/27, vs. Chiefs 73 (100%) 0 57.5 51.1 71.3 10/4, @ Vikings 39 (100%) 0 51.2 48.6 64.9 10/11, vs. Bengals 66 (100%) 0 72.7 74.9 52.2 BYE 10/25, @ Jets 65 (100%) 0 59.6 58.2 61.3 DNP Jonah Savaiinaea Game Snap Counts Penalties PFF Overall Grade PFF Run Blocking PFF Pass Protection 9/13, @ Raiders 59 (100%) 0 47.6 50.9 38.2 9/20, @ 49ers 56 (100%) 0 65.9 68.5 46.1 9/27, vs. Chiefs 73 (100%) 0 56.6 58.4 47.5 10/4, @ Vikings 39 (100%) 0 49.5 44.6 77.5 10/11, vs. Bengals 18 (27%) 0 45.4 44.7 78.4 BYE 10/25, @ Jets 65 (100%) 0 49.4 53,5 31.4 11/1, vs. Patriots 65 (100%) 1 49.7 51.9 63.4 What We Learned The first thing we learned is that the offensive line was out of sorts without Kadyn Proctor. Maybe it was a coincidence, the result of good defensive scheming or an intentionally deflated football (#neverforget), but the offensive line never seemed to operate as a cohesive unit against the Patriots. And the stats back that up. Not that sacks and run efficiency tell the whole story, but let’s look at the team performance since Week 4, when Ollie Gordon first took over as the featured running back: Week 4: Gordon, 9 rushes, 100 yards (11.1 ypc); 2 sacks allowed Week 5: Gordon, 18 rushes, 88 yards (4.9 ypc); 3 sacks allowed Week 7 following the bye: Gordon, 25 rushes, 103 yards (4.1 ypc); 2 sacks allowed And against the Patriots? Week 8: Gordon, 19 rushes, 69 yards (3.6 ypc); 5 sacks allowed As a team, the Dolphins’ yards-per-carry was a season-low 3.2 last Sunday. How much of that dip in performance is due to Proctor’s absence? It’s hard to say for sure, but I’m sure we’re all happy Proctor has cleared concussion protocol and is back in the lineup against the Lions. As for Jonah Savaiinaea, this was also a game to forget. Not only did he pick up his first penalty of the season (a holding call in the second quarter), but his overall PFF grade was the lowest of this week’s five starters on the offensive line, including Proctor’s replacement, Jarrett Kingston. Just looking at the PFF trends above, after his two best games in September against the 49ers and Chiefs, he’s turned in below-average grades in each of his last four appearances. Even if you’re not a believer in PFF grading, OL Coach Eric Smith in his weekly YouTube offensive line review (see the link below) also noted that Savaiinaea’s play has fallen off since September, and that his performance last week was reminiscent of 2025, when Jonah was statistically one of the worst guards in the league. My theory is that because the lines (offensive and defensive) function more as a unit, their performance is going to be impacted more by the absence of a starter than, say, the wide receiver room. I guess we can put that theory to the test this Sunday. The tracker will be updated each week throughout the season. For a more in-depth breakdown of Proctor’s and Savaiinaea’s performance, check out offensive line Coach Eric Smith’s film analysis of the game, which you can find on his YouTube channel, Focused on Fins .

This season, the Dolphins are focused on improving week to week and laying the foundation for future success. While they sit at 1-6 for the year, they fight each and every week, playing hard until the final whistle, a great sign for a team with 14 rookies and in the midst of a complete franchise rebuild. The Lions come into Sunday’s Week 9 game with a 5-2 record and looking like a team that can make a deep run in the NFC playoffs. After a disappointing 9-8 record in 2025 leading to a fourth-place finish in the NFC North, Detroit is looking to return to the form that brought them back-to-back division titles in 2023 and 2024. The NFC North is a tough division, however, with all four teams above the .500 mark and having won at least five times already this season. How will Sunday’s game play out? This feels like a game that could get away from the Dolphins, a byproduct of how diametrically opposed their 2026 trajectories are. The oddsmakers at FanDuel Sportsbook , however, seem to think this game might be a little tighter than might be expected. Phins up! Dive into game day on the SB Nation app! Celebrate every score and talk through every twist and turn with fellow Dolphins fans in real time. Join the live game chat Browse with fewer ads Seamlessly explore communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Lions (-6.5) at Dolphins Over the last two weeks, I was right on my prediction of the Dolphins beating the Jets straight-up, and on Miami losing to New England but covering the spread. This week, I am not as bullish on the Dolphins’ chances. The Lions are the better team in this matchup, and I think they’ll cover the 6.5-point spread, even with the injuries they are facing. Miami will play the Lions tough, and they might keep it close for much of the game, but in the end, I think the Lions pull away. Prop Bets Any time touchdown scorer: Ollie Gordon II Yes: +100 The Dolphins running game ran into a speedbump against the Patriots. After averaging 125 yards rushing in their last five games, Miami was held to just 74 yards in Week 8. They have to correct that in Week 9. It will not be easy, Detroit has the ninth-ranked rush defense in the league, allowing just 96.6 yards per game. The Dolphins will have to be deliberate in getting the ball to Gordon, continue to feed him even if they are getting stuffed early, and make this a physical game. In the end, I think Gordon will be able to find the endzone at least once in this game and this prop hits. Sam LaPorta receiving yards: 48.5 Over : -114 Under: -114 Miami has struggled covering tight ends this season, and they face another who could cause problems in LaPorta. They have allowed four tight ends to surpass the 48.5 yards mark (T.J. Hockenson, 119 yards; George Kittle, 80 yards; Mason Taylor, 62 yards; Travis Kelce, 59 yards) and would have had five on that list if Hunter Henry had not been injured in the second quarter Patriots game (3 receptions, 30 yards when he departed). Unless Miami comes with a different scheme to handle tight ends, LaPorta reaching 49 yards receiving seems likely. Chris Bell longest reception: 13.5 Over: 122 Under: -108 Bell is averaging 12.3 yards per catch, but the rookie has not been the primary target in the passing game – where Malik Washington has nearly double the amount of targets, almost three-times the receptions, and more than double the yards. Bell has been targeted more than fellow rookie Caleb Douglas – in part because Douglas missed three games with an injury – but Douglas has one more reception and almost 80 more yards than Bell. Miami is playing it smart with Bell, who tore his ACL less than a year ago, but it has depressed some of his stats this season. title: Miami Dolphins vs. Detroit Lions: Three Reasons Why
summary: The Miami Dolphins will be back in Joe Robbie Hard Rock Stadium to face the Detroit Lions this Sunday.  The good news? For the first time all season, the Dolphins will not have to go back out onto the road after a home game.  The bad news?  They face a hot Detroit Lions team.  Do […]
full_text: The Miami Dolphins will be back in Joe Robbie Hard Rock Stadium to face the Detroit Lions this Sunday. The good news? For the first time all season, the Dolphins will not have to go back out onto the road after a home game. The bad news? They face a hot Detroit Lions team. Do they have a chance? Mebbe . 3 REASONS FOR HOPE MALIK WILLIS IS IMPROVING Locked On Dolphins covered an aspect of this much more deeply than I can in an article, so I’ll let you watch for yourself . Willis was nothing short of atrocious the 1st 5 games. He had moments but was overall bad. But in the past 2 games, we have seen Willis take a step forward. I’ve listed my preferred stats in previous posts so let’s compare Willis’ 1st 5 games to the last 2 games in those stats. In the 1st five games, Willis had a completion percentage of 56.2% – completing 73 of his 130 attempts. In the last 2 games, Willis has a completion percentage of 66% – completing 35 of 53 pass attempts. In the 1st five games, Willis had a YPA of 6.53. In the last 2 games, he has a YPA of 7.91. He threw 2 TDs on 130 attempts for a TD% of 1.5%. In the last 2 games, he has 4 TDs on 53 attempts, for a TD% of 7.5%. Weeks 1-5, he had 4 INTs in 130 attempts for an INT% of 3.1%. The last 2 weeks, he has 1 INT in 53 attempts, which is an INT% of 1.9%. This is drastic improvement across the board. Two games don’t erase the previous five and I’m not saying he has suddenly gone from Joe Dirt to Joe Montana. But I said in the offseason he should be considered an “experienced rookie”. And like most rookies, there has been bumps in the road but also some growth. The next step is to maintain that growth and sustain these increased averages. But not only is there statistical improvement, he has become a vocal leader. Willis is a reserved man and doesn’t have a fiery disposition. But his interaction with Ollie Gordon II on the sideline after Gordon’s penalty and what was said after that shows a level of leadership I haven’t seen from a Dolphins’ quarterback in YEARS. It’s an impressive display for a young QB trying to find his footing and become a great player and a franchise QB. They don’t HAVE to listen to him, but that interaction shows that they do. THE REST OF THE OFFENSE IS GETTING BETTER The Dolphins started the season very rough on the offensive side of the ball. The were averaging 11.5 PPG the 1st 4 weeks of the season. In the last 3 games, they average 23.7 PPG. That would be 12th best if that were the season. In the 1st 4 games, they average 267.5 yards per game. In the last 3 games, they averaged 320 yards per game. Getting Caleb Douglas back helped, but we’ve also seen development and improvement from other WRs like Malik Washington – who is creating more separation than I would have expected – and Kevin Coleman Jr., who roasted a Pats DB for his 2nd TD of the season. Greg Dulcich is getting more involved. Gordon had a rougher day at the office against a stout NE run defense, but he is still on pace for a 1000-yard season and maybe he gets double digit TDs. It’s a young and growing offense that will have its fair share of issues, like we saw in the 3rd quarter last week. But they are getting better and now face… THE LIONS DEFENSE IS STRUGGLING So far this season, the Dolphins have faced 4 of the top 10 scoring defenses. They have faced 4 of the top 10 passing defenses in passing yards allowed. They have faced 3 of the top 10 rushing defenses in yards per attempt allowed. The Lions will not be any of those. The Lions have the 31st ranked pass defense in yards allowed, with 1936, and 32nd in passing yards per game allowed at 276.6. They are 26th in passer rating allowed at 101.0, 22nd in completion percentage allowed at 65.9, and 19th in YPA allowed at 7.3. They are tied for last with 18 passing TDs allowed. They have the 2nd highest ADOT for defender at 9.5, meaning teams are passing deeper on them. They are solid tacklers, with the fewest missed tackles at 15 and are 5th in YAC allowed, but the Dolphins should have some success in the air against the Lions. On the ground, the Lions are 6th in rushing yards allowed at 676 but also have the 3rd fewest attempts against them at 163. They allow 96.6 rushing yards per game and allowed 4.1 YPC. As a scoring defense, the Lions rank just ahead of Miami (25.9 PPG), allowing 25.7 PPG. Miami’s offense will have opportunities to move the ball and score. 3 REASONS FOR CONCERN THE LIONS’ PASS RUSH IS STILL STRONG Overall, the Lions’ defense looks like a weakness Miami could exploit. But the Lions can get after the QB very well. The Lions have 3 players with 4 or more sacks, led by standout edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson. One of those players is IDL Alim McNeill and strong interior pass rushers have given Miami issues. McNeill is ESPN’s top IDL pass rusher, with a win rate of 27%. As a team, the Lions rank 3rd in PRWR at 59%. Perhaps Kadyn Proctor’s return can mitigate that problem, but after last week, I’m skeptical. The Lions as a team are third in sacks with 24 and tied for 10th in pressure percentage at 24.8%. The Lions don’t blitz at a high rate, ranking 17th at 25.7%, so most of those pressures are generated with a 4-man rush. Miami’s OL will need to play much better than last week if they want to capitalize on the weaknesses of the Lions defense. MIAMI’S PASS RUSH FACES A TOUGH TEST The Dolphins’ defense has slowly started to move up the rankings of pressure percentage, currently 22nd at 21.1%. They are still on the bottom of the barrel in terms of sacks, tied with KC and NYG with 9. However, they have had at least 2 sacks in 3 of the past 4 games. Chop Robinson has come on with 4 sacks and leads the league in pressure percentage individually and has the best pass rush win rate . Unfortunately, the Lions have one of the best OLs in the league at stopping pressure. They rank 7th as a team in PBWR at 54% (see the previous link). PFF ranks them 1st and highlighted that the Lions’ OL only allowed 4 pressures last week to the league leading Vikings, who get a pressure 35% of the time. Both of Detroit’s OTs are top 20 in PBWR (Paul has dropped out of the top 20). The Dolphins and Jeff Hafley may need to get creative with pressure packages and blitz plans in order to get to Jared Goff. THE LIONS ARE A VERY DANGEROUS OFFENSE The Dolphins have faced some scary offenses this season, but none present the total package that Detroit presents. The Chiefs have Mahomes and Walker, but don’t have elite receivers. Cincy has Burrow and elite WRs, but their run game isn’t special. The Lions have all of it. They’re 4th in the league in total yards at 2768, but the 3 teams ahead of them have played an additional game. They average 395.4 yards per game and 5.9 yards per play, tied for 5th. They are 4th in passing yards per game at 264.0 and 7th in rushing yards per game at 131.4. Goff is completing 67.7% of his passes, 5th best. He’s thrown 15 TDs and only 1 INT. Jahmyr Gibbs is 2nd in the league in attempts with 157, and 2nd in rushing yards with 773. He has 8 rushing TDs, tied with several for 3rd, and leads the league in both yards per game at 110.4 and attempts per game at 22.4. Gibbs also has 2 receiving TDs. Amon-Ra St. Brown is 5th in the league in receptions with 53, 10th in yards with 571, and tied for 6th in TDs with 5. One of those he is tied with is his teammate Jameson Williams. Williams doesn’t have the volume, with only 27 catches, but has 437 yards, meaning a 16.2 YPC average. Of WRs with more than 20 catches, only Tee Higgins, Christian Watson, Rome Odunze, and Tre Tucker have a higher YPC average. TE Sam LaPorta is tied with Williams and Gibbs in targets with 44 and has added 31 catches, 367 yards, and 3 TDs. Those 4 players are Detroit’s primary weapons. Only one other RB on the team – Sione Vaki – has any rushing attempts and all other pass catchers have 36 combined targets. The Lions know who they are, what they have, and they lean heavily on it. They are successful with it.…

title: 5 Things I Think I Think About the Miami Dolphins After Week 8
summary: Let’s start with the bad news. The Miami Dolphins are 1-6, having scored the second-fewest points in the entire league. (Who’s scored the fewest? Thank you for asking. It’s the winless Los Angeles Chargers, whose offense is led by our old friend, Mike McDaniel. There’s a lesson in there somewhere.) Young, developing teams can be […]
full_text: Let’s start with the bad news. The Miami Dolphins are 1-6, having scored the second-fewest points in the entire league. (Who’s scored the fewest? Thank you for asking. It’s the winless Los Angeles Chargers, whose offense is led by our old friend, Mike McDaniel. There’s a lesson in there somewhere.) Young, developing teams can be hard to watch sometimes, but they can also be rewarding if you know what to look for. So with that in mind, here are five things I think I think after Week 8. There’s a Good Team in There Somewhere For one glorious half, the Dolphins looked like a quality, well-coached football team. Their defense forced a fumble deep in Patriots territory. After trading field goals through most of the first half, they drove 70 yards for a touchdown, spreading the ball around to Greg Dulcich, Caleb Douglas and Kevin Coleman before connecting with Malik Washington for a short touchdown just before the break. Perhaps unsurprisingly, things unraveled in the second half. The Patriots made adjustments the Dolphins couldn’t counter, and (as we’ll discuss shortly) Miami made so many self-inflicted mistakes that it couldn’t overcome them. But it’s hard not to wonder: If the Dolphins can build a double-digit lead over a playoff contender like the Patriots while making so many unforced errors, what happens when they stop making them? That Said, the Dolphins Are Still Making Rookie Mistakes Playing against a Mike Vrabel-led team isn’t going to be easy. Any lapses in communication on either side of the ball are going to be exploited, and the Dolphins weren’t exactly on their A game. On one of Malik Willis’ five (!) sacks, Douglas and Bell ended up running to … the same area of the field. After stopping the Patriots’ offense to open the second half, the Dolphins had a chance to extend their lead. Instead, on third-and-9, Willis’ pass at the sticks doinked off Dulcich’s helmet. And at the end of the third quarter, two defenders covered the option on Drake Maye’s goal-line read-option, leaving Maye free to waltz untouched into the end zone. It didn’t cost them much, I suppose, but a wide-open Jaylen Wright also dropped an easy pass. (And no, I’m not emotionally ready to talk about Ollie Gordon’s unsportsmanlike penalty.) These are fixable mistakes, but they cost the Dolphins a winnable game against a division opponent. Malik Willis Is Becoming Part of the Solution OK, so 19 points doesn’t seem like much of an answer to the torches-and-pitchforks crowd around these parts three weeks ago. And even after two games of noticeable improvement, I don’t think we’re anywhere near being able to say, “Hey, let’s not spend an early-round 2027 pick on a quarterback.” That said, 21-of-32 for 211 yards, two touchdowns and a deflected interception? That’s “pass”able (ha ha) for a quarterback playing with little help from the running game and under pressure for much of the afternoon. More to the point, Willis is starting to do what professional quarterbacks do: throw the ball away, take the easy yards when they’re there and avoid putting the ball in harm’s way. (Though I see we’re still sliding behind the line of scrimmage for a sack instead of throwing the ball away, so there’s still some growth that needs to happen.) It’s a small thing, but a necessary one if you want to see continued development. I’m eager to see how he performs against the Lions this week. Kadyn Proctor’s Importance Is No Longer Theoretical In my Tracking the Guards series, I’ve talked a lot about how people who understand offensive line play have been impressed with Proctor’s development this year, even if his PFF grades don’t always reflect it. But if you really want to judge how well a player is performing, look at how the team does when he’s not in the lineup. Proctor missed the Patriots game while in concussion protocol. His replacement, Jarrett Kingston, played fine, but Proctor’s absence was noticeable. Without him, the Dolphins’ running game lacked its power. There were far fewer instances of linebackers getting neutralized, and the Patriots’ safeties and second-level defenders had a much easier time disrupting the offense. Proctor is expected back in the lineup against the Lions, and it’s clear the team needs him. It’s Not Always Pretty, but the Rebuild Seems To Be Working Just look at all the players 25 or younger who are either starting or playing meaningful snaps: Patrick Paul. Caleb Douglas. Malik Washington. Kevin Coleman. Chris Bell. Kadyn Proctor. Jacob Rodriguez. Michael Taaffe. Chris Johnson. Chop Robinson. Jordan Phillips. Jonah Savaiinaea. You could probably throw in Kenny Grant, Dante Trader, Jason Marshall and Zeek Biggers, too. That’s an incredible amount of development time, and it’s time that isn’t being spent (or wasted) on players like Jonnu Smith or Jalen Ramsey. And, with a few notable exceptions, they’ve largely stayed healthy, too. They’re getting the reps they need to grow into the players we want them to be. Those reps are also producing penalties and blown assignments, but that’s part of the growth process, too. So, yeah, 1-6 isn’t much fun, and it’s definitely not fun listening to pundits talk about how the Dolphins’ future opponents are going to have a field day playing them. But the growth and talent development are exciting to watch, and to me, much more rewarding than what we’ve seen in recent years: older players underperforming and getting hurt. I like this version better.

LP = Limited participant in practice. DNP = Did not participate in practice. NIR = Not injury related. PUP = Physically unable to participate list. IR = Injured reserve. Note: only starters on IR are listed. Player Name* = Starter. Injury designation definitions: Probable = the league defines a Probable injury designation as a 75% or greater chance of playing. Historically, 95% of players designated probable are active and played on game day. Questionable = the league defines a Questionable injury designation as being ‘uncertain’ of whether the player will play or not. This replaces the former definition of having a 50% chance of playing. Historically, 70-75% of players with a Questionable injury designation were active and played on game day. Doubtful = The league defines a Doubtful injury designation to mean the player is unlikely to participate in the game. In practical terms, teams use the designation when a player has less than a 50% chance to suit up, and active game appearances from this designation remain rare. Historically only around 6% of players with a Doubtful designation are active and played on game day. Out = will not play. Players with this designation are not active on game day and league rules prohibit them from playing. Notes on Injured Players For the Vikings, Kyler Murray is out as expected, as are both Demond Claiborne and Jauan Jennings. Claiborne suffered a knee injury in practice and from Kevin O’Connell’s comments on Saturday, could be out for a while. It wouldn’t be surprising therefore if he was placed on Injured Reserve. It doesn’t appear at the moment that Jennings’ calf injury is a longer-term concern, but we may learn more about that next week. Beyond that, safeties Theo Jackson and Jay Ward are questionable for Monday night. I’m guessing at least one of them will play, but KOC also talked about potentially having Jacob Thomas and/or Tavierre Thomas on the active roster for Monday night to fill in at safety and special teams. For the Bills, backup wide receiver Joshua Palmer is out. But they also have two starting offensive linemen listed as questionable- left tackle Dion Dawkins and left guard Alec Anderson. Dawkins has not practiced all week with a rib injury, so he would seem to be less likely than normal to start with that designation. Anderson was upgraded to limited on Saturday after missing Thursday and Friday practices with an ankle injury. My guess is that if either of them play on Monday night they will be less than 100%, so the left side of the Bills’ offensive line could be a bit more vulnerable than normal. Beyond that, Tyrell Shavers and Jordan Hancock are listed as questionable, but the Bills will need to activate them from the PUP list and IR for them to be eligible to play on Monday night. We’ll see if that happens. Follow me on X/Bluesky @wludford

Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images We’ve got our SB Nation Reacts results for this week ready to roll, so let’s take a look at what fans of the Minnesota Vikings have to say about our favorite team this week, shall we? Our first question for this week, as it always is, has to do with whether or not everyone is confident with the direction of the team. And, coming after the first loss of the season in Week 8, the answer is a resounding, “No. . .no, we are not.” Of those who responded to our poll for this week, just 17% are confident that a team currently sporting a 6-1 record is moving in the right direction. On the surface, that sounds a bit absurd, but honestly. . .it’s not terribly difficult to understand. The offense, once again, struggled to score against a defense that it really shouldn’t have struggled against, and the defense eventually just wore down as the offense wasn’t able to stay on the field. It’s the same formula that we’ve seen repeatedly this season, and something has to change going forward. And, a few days ago, something did. Which leads us to our second question for a week, which asked about whether or not the team needed to make a change at quarterback. Now, keep in mind that we posted this question before the team formally made the announcement that Carson Wentz would start at quarterback against the Buffalo Bills on Monday, but I’m not sure how much it would have affected the results. Of those who responded to our poll, 78% agreed that a change needed to be made at quarterback in some form. There were 45% who said that the Vikings should go to Wentz, which is what has happened. . .so far. Another 33% believe that the Vikings should make a trade, which is something that could still happen before the NFL trade deadline, which arrives this Tuesday at 3:00 PM Central Time. The other 22% believe that the Vikings should stay the course at quarterback, which simply tells me that there were more Bears, Lions, and Packers fans voting in the poll than usual this week. As a bit of a bonus question this week, GA Skol has put a poll over in the feed about whether or not the shift to Wentz gives the Vikings a better chance to win on Monday night against the Bills. Those are our SB Nation Reacts results for this week, ladies and gentlemen!
