title: Run game, not quarterback, is the offensive key to ‘Seahawks Football’
summary: This has been a challenging year for the Seattle Seahawks. Maybe we should’ve known it would be that way when Sam Darnold was injured just mere snaps into the season. Drew Lock stepped in admirably leading Seattle to victories in the first two weeks. When Darnold came back earlier than most expected, it looked like […]
full_text: This has been a challenging year for the Seattle Seahawks. Maybe we should’ve known it would be that way when Sam Darnold was injured just mere snaps into the season . Drew Lock stepped in admirably leading Seattle to victories in the first two weeks. When Darnold came back earlier than most expected, it looked like things were going to get back on track. Then, the maelstrom of turnovers and injuries hit, leaving Seattle looking rudderless at 4-4. Darnold is injured once again , and his long-term future with the Seahawks is (rightly) being questioned. John Schneider has done this before, pivoting from both Russell Wilson and Geno Smith. Regardless of who is taking snaps under center, Mike Macdonald wants to play “Seahawks Football.” He’s referenced that multiple times this year, and used it when discussing his hire of offensive coordinator Brian Fleury. The idea is to have a system that is replicable and not reliant on specific personnel. More specifically, “Seahawks Football” needs a strong run game as the backbone. Even just the threat of the run alleviates the pressure from the passing offense. Seattle hasn’t had the luxury of that in 2026 due to a litany of issues including poor blocking, fumbles, injuries, etc. The low hanging fruit is to bring up the defection of Ken Walker III. Yes, his departure is part of the reason for the struggling rushing attack, but I think even he would have a tough time running behind this offensive line. After a giant step forward with line play last season, expectations were extremely high for this year with all five starters returning. Anthony Bradford was injured early on, and the rest of the line seemed to regress and struggle. Quenton Nelson was brought in as part of the solution , but his addition created new problems that reared their ugly heads in the crapstorm against the Chicago Bears. Backup left tackle, new left guard Grey Zabel moving to the right side for the first time in the NFL, two running backs returning from injury. That kinda seems like a recipe for disaster, doesn’t it? And disaster ensued as the offense was ineffective in everything except the “throw it to JSN” play. When Nelson was acquired from the Indianapolis Colts, many were wondering why they traded him weeks before the trade deadline when they could’ve possibly gotten a bigger return down the line. I’m not going to say Seattle sacrificed the game against Chicago, but the three weeks following that are matchups against the Arizona Cardinals, Las Vegas Raiders, and the bye week with a huge rematch against the San Francisco 49ers looming. Having Quenton Nelson and Grey Zabel broken into their new teams/positions at that point for the stretch run is pivotal. Jadarian Price and Zach Charbonnet should also be rounding into form by then. The injury to Nelson throws a monkey wrench into things, but the theory would still be that the Seahawks run game should be improved coming out of the bye week. Mike Macdonald’s vision of “Seahawks Football” is not to throw the football 40 times a game. Control the game by moving the sticks on the ground, supplement with explosive passes, and play tough defense. That’s how the Seahawks were successful when they were on their Super Bowl run last season. Hell, that was the blueprint for Pete Carroll’s Seahawks as well. It’s a proven formula that works. The key to getting back on track starts with the OL and RB room, not who will be taking snaps be it Sam Darnold, Drew Lock, or Jalen Milroe. I still believe that Macdonald wants a QB who can be an asset in the run game. His time in Baltimore with Lamar Jackson showed him just how dangerous a dual threat QB can be. After Milroe was drafted, Macdonald spoke on that topic. “Quarterbacks who can extend the play are incredibly difficult to defend,” Macdonald said. “The worst thing in the world is you play the first (part) of the play perfectly on defense, and you’re like, ‘All right, sweet, we did it.’ And the guy still has the ball, and you’ve got to defend the next play, and then sometimes a third play. “He can kill you in the first play, he can kill you in the second play, he can kill you in the third play. It’s not a fun existence to live in consistently. He has that ability.” I swear that I read somewhere after that draft that Milroe was a Mike Macdonald pick, but I haven’t been able to find it. That would make a ton of sense, however, given Macdonald’s time playing against Baltimore and his history/respect for the armed forces, of which Milroe’s father was a part of just like Macdonald’s. Maybe Milroe isn’t the answer as the QB for Seattle, but I have a gut feeling that Macdonald wants a QB that can break the game open with his legs as well. Yeah, so does everyone else, I get it. A QB that can accentuate the run game makes the offense so much harder to defend. If it gives the defensive wunderkind Macdonald problems, you can bet it’s an issue for everyone else. That brings us back to the crux of the issue. Seattle’s run game just isn’t good enough right now to carry the team, and it needs to be. Forget worrying about a repeat. Don’t fret about playoffs. If the Seahawks can fix the run game everything will take care of itself. That’s the formula for replicable success that will bring Seattle back into championship contention no matter who the QB is. That’s “Seahawks Football” .

title: Seahawks discussion: Fans predict Sam Darnold’s future
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Seahawks fans and fans across the country. full_text: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Seahawks fans and fans across the country. Sign up here to participate in the weekly emailed surveys. There is little doubt the 2026 season for the Seattle Seahawks has not gone to plan. Many fans, myself included, had high hopes. Brian Fleury had a unique background involving offense, defense, special teams and Kyle Shanahan mentorship. Most of the starters on the team remained. Darnold, who does well in the Shanahan style offense looked poised to continue his 2024-2025 success. Now, the team being 4-4 and while the defense has help up its end still being a top three unit, and special teams being top 15 or higher depending on the metric, the offense outside of Jaxon-Smith Njigba has been less stellar. This leaves fans wondering: How confident are we in this team? Will Darnold be the quarterback still in 2027? We asked you those very questions. Let’s see where you, the fans, landed. Just 33 percent of fans believe Sam Darnold will be the quarterback next season. This is understandable. He has struggled this season, and is now out with his second set of injuries this season . How much of his struggles are on him, and how much of it is due to Fleury, the scheme he has imposed on the offense, and his play calling, that is for fans to decide. We all have our opinions, and ultimately, only they know the truth. Sam Darnold was 30th out of 33 qualifying QBs in EPA/dropback when pressured, but he was also one of the least pressured QBs in the NFL last year. He's 31st out of 31 QBs in EPA/dropback when pressured in 2026, and he's top 12 in pressure rate. — Mookie Alexander (@mookiealexander) November 3, 2026 The fact is, Darnold has not looked comfortable in this offense, and it looks as thought the offensive players have been struggling with the new play calling and scheme. The offensive line has regressed, receivers are dropping catches they normally catch, and Darnold is getting pressured more than he did in 2025. That is not a recipe for success for any quarterback. As far as fan confidence, 27 percent of fans are headed in the right direction, and I am convinced this is due to the offensive struggles. Whether Mike Macdonald and John Schneider want to admit it or not, from the fan perspective, they chose poorly when it came to the offensive coordinator. Through eight games, the only game that seemingly was called well was versus the Kansas City Chiefs. One out of eight games. Not great odds. They have the Arizona Cardinals next, and the injury report looks like an obituary. Seahawks injury report ahead of their Week 9 game vs. Arizona: pic.twitter.com/Rr7SwV5iMr — John Boyle (@johnpboyle) November 6, 2026 This will be a true test for the team. Some big time leaders are out, and the Seahawks will need to truly be prepared. The “next man up” mentality needs to pull through, or the 73 percent of fans who do not believe the Seahawks are headed in the right direction, and those who believe in the Hard Knocks curse will have more evidence to add to their collection. title: 49ers vs. Raiders: How to watch, game time, and betting odds
summary: The bye week is over, and the San Francisco 49ers are back to football for Week 9. This week, they’ll welcome a once-familiar foe as the Las Vegas Raiders return to California. I say “once” familiar because, as you know, the Raiders were once based in Oakland and the Battle of the Bay was a […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - AUGUST 27: Adrian Martinez #4 of the San Francisco 49ers is forced out of bounds by Tommy Eichenberg #44 of the Las Vegas Raiders in the second quarter of their preseason game at Allegiant Stadium on August 27, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. The 49ers defeated the Raiders 18-12. (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The bye week is over, and the San Francisco 49ers are back to football for Week 9. This week, they’ll welcome a once-familiar foe as the Las Vegas Raiders return to California. I say “once” familiar because, as you know, the Raiders were once based in Oakland and the Battle of the Bay was a regular thing. One that came with some interesting fan experiences in the past. With the Raiders in Vegas, it’s a bit different, but the rivalry may be the same. This will be an afternoon game; Kevin Kugler has the play-by-play, and Daryl Johnston will provide color. The 49ers went into their bye week suffering their first loss of the season at the hands of the Atlanta Falcons. The 49ers did not look good in any phase of that game, committing costly turnovers and suffering bonehead penalties. It didn’t help that running back Christian McCaffrey was limited in the game and Mike Evans did not play at all. The defense failed to generate consistent pressure against the Falcons offense. Fortunately, help is on the way as the 49ers traded for DeForest Buckner from the Indianapolis Colts. Since the trade happened last week, Buckner has had plenty of time to acclimate to Raheem Morris and the 49ers defense. Buckner last played with the 49ers in 2019 when Robert Saleh was defensive coordinator. The Raiders surprised everyone opening the season with three straight wins. These were wins over the Miami Dolphins, Los Angeles Chargers, and New Orleans Saints, teams that have issues not as severe as the Raiders. After that string of victories, the Raiders lost four straight to the Kansas City Chiefs, New England Patriots, Buffalo Bills, and Los Angeles Rams. The point is that the Raiders can beat bad teams, but they can’t beat good teams. That doesn’t mean they can’t hang around; two of those losses were by three points. The Raiders have weapons and can surprise you, but if the schedule is any indication, when they go up against better talent, they can’t hang in there. There’s also Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins. Cousins has a history of making life miserable for the 49ers—at least when he was with the Minnesota Vikings. In a 2023 Monday Night Football game, Cousins went 35 for 45 (77.8 percent completion) for 378 yards, two touchdowns, and one interception. Could Cousins’ stats be different with the Raiders? Only one way to find out. The 49ers’ injuries have grown worse; wide receiver Christian Kirk was placed on Injured Reserve Saturday, most likely putting an end to his season (and time with the 49ers). Wide receiver Demarcus Robinson was activated Saturday as well, so there are some positives. Further complicating matters are wide receiver Mike Evans (Achilles) and Deebo Samuel (hamstring), both but. Cornerbacks Upton Stout (neck) and Nate Hobbs (adductor) as well as Safety Siran Neal (knee/foot) are listed as questionable. The Rams will be without defensive tackle Thomas Booker (ankle). Cornerback Darien Porter (groin) is questionable. title: 49ers activate Demarcus Robinson, place Christian Kirk on Injured Reserve
summary: The San Francisco 49ers have made their roster moves in preparation for their game against the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday. The team announced that they have activated wide receiver Demarcus Robinson. They also removed Robinson’s questionable game status for the Raiders. While there’s some help on the way for the wide receivers, the position […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 25: Christian Kirk #3 of the San Francisco 49ers runs with the ball against the Atlanta Falcons prior to an NFL football game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers have made their roster moves in preparation for their game against the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday. The team announced that they have activated wide receiver Demarcus Robinson. They also removed Robinson’s questionable game status for the Raiders. While there’s some help on the way for the wide receivers, the position takes another hit as Christian Kirk has been placed on Injured Reserve. Kirk was already ruled out for Sunday’s game after hurting his meniscus during Thursday’s practice. The severity of the injury wasn’t fully known, but if he’s going to the injured reserve book list, that says all you need to know. The 49ers can only bring back so many players from IR so adding yet another name to an already deep list means that’s one less player that can come back when they are ready. To keep on with the wide receiver news, the 49ers also announced that KhaDarel Hodge will be activated from the practice squad for Sunday. Shanahan wasn’t sure about this after his press conference Friday, but it seems like the 49ers had little choice with Kirk’s IR designation. With Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel already out, expect to see more of Demarcus Robinson. He was a big target for Brock Purdy in Week 1 against the Los Angeles Rams, so hopefully he can pick right up where he left off. The 49ers certainly need some wide receiver help until they can get some of their weapons back.

title: 49ers Mailbag: Should the team get more defensive line help? What’s up with the return/kicking game?
summary: What? You mean you guys like these things? We haven’t done too many mailbags this year, but maybe I can change that. Because of the timing, I wasn’t able to get to every question asked in my call for submissions, but keep an eye out for the next one. I post over in the Niners […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - DECEMBER 23: DeForest Buckner #99 of the San Francisco 49ers in action during the game against the Chicago Bears at Levi Stadium on December 23, 2018 in Santa Clara, CA. The Bears defeated the 49ers 14-9. (Photo by Rob Leiter/Getty Images) | Getty Images What? You mean you guys like these things? We haven’t done too many mailbags this year, but maybe I can change that. Because of the timing, I wasn’t able to get to every question asked in my call for submissions, but keep an eye out for the next one. I post over in the Niners Nation Feed when I’m going to do a mailbag, and I’ll be sure to not do it on a Thursday this time. By the way, if you haven’t gone to The Feed yet, what’s stopping you? Not only am I there, but Fooch posts there a lot, too. Come hang out with the Niners Nation alum! Now, as for this week, this is going up Saturday afternoon, and the San Francisco 49ers are preparing for the Las Vegas Raiders. This seems like another tricky game for the team. Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins always seems to play well against the 49ers, like some long-standing grudge against Kyle Shanahan when the former was going to come in a few years before the latter traded for Jimmy Garoppolo. I think the 49ers can pull off the victory—based on the Raiders starting to remember they are the Raiders—but they can’t make the same mistakes they did against the Atlanta Falcons. Ok, onto your questions: If a Pontiac and a Buick both leave Chicago at the same time………. —NYners They both will have engine failure two miles outside of city limits. And keeping with the STs theme — why do they still have faith in Cowing returning punts? I’m terrified he’s gonna drop it, even on a fair catch. If the former Ram who’s on the practice squad isn’t any better, why do we even have him on the team? —TheGoldenRatio Probably because they don’t want to pull from the very limited pool of wide receivers they already have and risk someone else getting beat up on the return game. I have to think that as the wide receivers come back, the 49ers move to…well…moving on from Cowing. At least at returner. They have Brandin Cooks on the roster, and while he’s not as fast as he was a decade ago, he’s still got some wheels and has been a returner in the past. De’Zhaun Stribling could also be a good option, but for reasons I just outlined, they may want him fresh for the offense and not on return duty because they aren’t going to be able to rely on Mike Evans for every play. I can’t fathom a situation where Cowing is the punt returner in January based on what we’ve seen. This isn’t even about his ball security issues; it’s about his decision-making. I’m of the mind that our D line is pretty awesome with Defo and Bosa on the field. My only reservation is injuries, especially Bosa. Do we really need to make a splash with an extra Edge? White, Williams and Height seems like a good rotation across from Bosa. — 80849er It could help, but I also think the 49ers need to hold onto some draft picks and salary cap space. Whoever they bring in, they have to make room for by releasing someone else, allocating what is the thinnest of margins in cap space, and sacrificing development of their younger talent. Not to mention draft picks. It’s not the greatest answer, but when they bring in a Khalil Mack or some sort, that’s going to take snaps away from a younger player who needs that experience and fewer picks to get more ammo in case that younger player doesn’t work out. I want to win now, just like all of you do, but not at the cost of development to stay competitive. I am not a fan of the Los Angeles’ Rams way of just “buying” a Super Bowl for one year. Some players you know won’t click; others need to be on the field and mess up, even in a championship season. The DeForest Buckner trade was great because while it removed snaps, it didn’t do so much that it tossed the depth chart to the bench. Adding more could make things cramped. It also helped with the culture since Buckner has been there before and can be a good mentor Speaking of which, that has already been paying dividends for young talent. Romello Height is getting up a bit earlier now , for one thing. The others have a lot to learn from Buckner as a player, and it’s already rubbing off. Has something changed in Piñeiro’s mechanics, or with the snap and hold timing? Is he more accurate from one hash mark or another? How does he compare to the league average percentage of missed extra points? Why hasn’t the team brought in another kicker for a tryout? Why haven’t they brought someone else in? Probably because Piñeiro just signed an extension with $10 million in guaranteed money. Kyle Shanahan did seem a bit miffed after the Atlanta game, but shortly after that, John Lynch affirmed the 49ers were sticking with Piñeiro. If you were wanting kicker tryouts—those aren’t happening. Have we hit David Akers or even Jake Moody levels of kicking? It’s a rough patch, but I give him a couple more games. If he misses more XPs in the next two games, regardless of whether it’s a victory or loss, the 49ers have to do something. It’s just like if their punt returner had bad ball security and they did nothing… Brandon Aiyuk owes the 49ers $13 million. If you’d signed that contract, what would you have spent the $13 million on? —Fooch I’d go to Vegas and make max bets on Casino War while getting bottle service. I’d set aside half for an executive suite at Levi’s Stadium for one game. I’d also buy a sealed copy of Panzer Dragoon Saga for the Sega Saturn. If there’s money leftover I’ll also buy a gold cart of Nintendo World Championships .

title: 5 questions with Silver and Black Pride: Is there any hope for the Raiders’ defense against the 49ers?
summary: Matt Holder from Silver and Black Pride helped us out this week with five questions about this week’s matchup between the San Francisco 49ers and the Las Vegas Raiders. We talked about Kyle Shanahan and Kirk Cousins, the Raiders’ defense against the Niners’ offense, Las Vegas’s running back situation, and Brock Bowers. 1) You can’t […]
full_text: (Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images) | Getty Images Matt Holder from Silver and Black Pride helped us out this week with five questions about this week’s matchup between the San Francisco 49ers and the Las Vegas Raiders. We talked about Kyle Shanahan and Kirk Cousins, the Raiders’ defense against the Niners’ offense, Las Vegas’s running back situation, and Brock Bowers. 1) You can’t tell the Kirk Cousins story without Kyle Shanahan. How surprising is it to see Cousins play this well, and do you think he’ll continue that this season, even if the Raiders remain one-dimensional? Heading into the season, I thought Cousins was going to be nothing more than a placeholder for Fernando Mendoza. So, I’m very shocked by how well he’s been playing and was dead wrong in the offseason. He’s one of the biggest reasons the Raiders are in the playoff picture at the halfway point of the season. You’re 100% correct that Vegas’ offense is one-dimensional, and the lack of a running game could lead to the 38-year-old starting to show his age down the stretch. But so far, there’s been no sign of regression from Cousins. He isn’t perfect; his age/lack of mobility and arm strength show up when under pressure, but he’s coming off his best game of the year last week against the Jets. 2) Is there any hope for the Raiders defense? Everybody scores against them. The 49ers won’t have Mike Evans, but it still seems like the Niners will move the ball up and down the field. How do you see the Raiders getting stops? Kyle Shanahan’s game plan can be pretty simple this week: line up in 12 or 13 personnel (or technically 21/22 personnel with Kyle Juszczyk) and pound the rock. Shanahan doesn’t even need Evans because Las Vegas’ defense can’t stop the run out of those formations. Even the Jets had success with that, as Braelon Allen averaged 7.0 yards per carry and set a career-high rushing yardage total in the first half. New York is just poorly coached and only ran the ball four times in the second half despite playing with a lead, allowing Vegas to come back in the fourth quarter. Also, the Raiders’ defense doesn’t have a legitimate answer for George Kittle. Not that tight ends have necessarily hurt them in the passing game all year, but Kittle is the best one the Raiders’ defense has faced, and the unit doesn’t have someone who I think can match up with him. Ultimately, I think San Francisco should have no problem putting up at least 30 points on Sunday. Vegas hasn’t kept an opponent under 30 since September, and the Saints put up 27 points in three quarters in Week 3. 3) What’s going on at running back? Do you think it was a mistake to take Jeanty? Did he already lose his job? Is it more about Mike Washington being good or Jeanty being bad? ESPN’s Dan Graziano reported this week that Jeanty getting two carries while Washington had 25 in New York was meant to serve as a “wake-up call” for the 2025 No. 6 overall pick. In other words, a ‘soft benching’. Also, Jeanty stupidly made a bulletin-board-material comment about the Jets’ defense — essentially saying they don’t like to tackle — so I think Klint Kubiak’s decision was at least partly punitive. Additionally, the Raiders’ running game has been terrible this season, as it was a year ago. Kubiak has tried different offensive line combinations, so he flipped the running back rotation to see how that works. Washington definitely didn’t run away with the starting job, but the offense was much better at staying on schedule with him toting the rock. The rookie doesn’t have great vision and will miss opportunities for big plays. But at least last week, he did a better job of getting what he can compared to Jeanty. Moving forward, I expect Washington to continue having a bigger workload, but I think the touches will be closer to 50/50. Personally, I’m not ready to give up on Jeanty. However, if another team was interested in giving up, say, a second-round pick for him either by Tuesday or in the offseason, I’d probably take that deal. He isn’t the biggest problem; the offensive line is, but he isn’t helping make the situation better. 4) Klint Kubiak was on the 49ers coaching staff a few years back. How do Raiders fans feel about Kubiak, and is there a real sense that he can lead this team to the playoffs in the near future? Some in Raider Nation are frustrated with Kubiak because the team started 3-0, giving some hope for the playoffs, only to see a four-game losing streak against playoff-caliber opponents in October. But I’d say those people are in the minority. Anyone who was sensible knew that this was going to be a rebuilding year for the Raiders, and they already have more wins in 2026 than 2025. That’s progress for an organization that had the No. 1 overall pick in the draft last April, especially since the No. 1 pick has barely seen the field. Sure, the Silver and Black haven’t beaten a quality opponent and are “frauds” when it comes to being a postseason contender this season. However, the team is headed in the right direction by separating itself from the bottom of the league. Overall, I think the majority of the fanbase is happy with Kubiak and feels he’s capable of leading them to the playoffs in the future. Again, this was supposed to be year one of a two-year rebuild, and the fact the Raiders are even in the postseason discussion at this stage makes it seem like the plan is ahead of schedule. 5) Is Brock Bowers better than George Kittle? Which skill players would you take over Bowers at this point? I know a trap question when I see one, LOL! Right now, I think Kittle is the better overall tight end since he’s basically a sixth offensive lineman in the running game. But to me, Bowers is the NFL’s most unique weapon in the passing game. He can beat both defensive backs and linebackers by getting open or making ridiculous contested catches and is used more like a ‘WR1’ than a typical tight end, commanding the attention of the opposing defense’s best coverage defender every week. Bowers creates a lot of matchup problems, similar to how Sean Payton used to use Jimmy Graham in New Orleans. To be honest, there aren’t many other skill players around the league that I’d take over the third-year offensive weapon. It’d have to be one of the top-tier wide receivers, like a Ja’Marr Chase or Justin Jefferson type. Bowers is just such a unicorn that it’d take a lot for me to want to give him up.
author: Kyle Posey

title: A’Shawn Robinson fined for late hit in Buccaneers’ Week 8 shutout win vs. Falcons
summary: The Atlanta Falcons had a very long day against the Buccaneers defense in Week 8. Michael Penix Jr. threw four interceptions and completed only 33% of his passes in the driving rain en route to a 16-0 win for Tampa Bay. In the third quarter, the Falcons had a first and 10 on their own […]
full_text: Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images | Getty Images The Atlanta Falcons had a very long day against the Buccaneers defense in Week 8. Michael Penix Jr. threw four interceptions and completed only 33% of his passes in the driving rain en route to a 16-0 win for Tampa Bay. In the third quarter, the Falcons had a first and 10 on their own 33. Penix’s pass intended for Khalil Herbert went incomplete, and A’Shawn Robinson was flagged for a late hit on Penix and penalized 15 yards. On Saturday, the NFL confirmed Robinson has also been fined $17,500 for the late hit . Robinson is the first Buccaneers player to be fined by the NFL since Bucky Irving was hit with a $6,988 fine for a chop block against the Vikings in Week 3. Those are the only two fines for Bucs players this season, The NFL donates half the funds it collects from player discipline to the NFLPA’s efforts to support retired players, and the other half goes to the NFL Foundation and other organizations that benefit youth football programs, community health initiatives, and player safety.

summary: Titans cornerback Alontae Taylor owes the NFL $23,882 in fines for unnecessary roughness in the Titans’ Week 8 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals. The fine information specifies that it’s for impermissible use of the helmet. The action Taylor was fined for wasn’t flagged in real time, but he was fined regardless. Taylor finished Sunday’s game […]
full_text: Photo by Jeff Dean/Getty Images | Getty Images Titans cornerback Alontae Taylor owes the NFL $23,882 in fines for unnecessary roughness in the Titans’ Week 8 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals. The fine information specifies that it’s for impermissible use of the helmet. The action Taylor was fined for wasn’t flagged in real time, but he was fined regardless. Taylor finished Sunday’s game with five total tackles, one tackle for loss, and two quarterback hits on Joe Burrow. It’s Taylor’s first fine of the 2026 season. The Titans went on to lose in overtime to the Bengals, 43-36. Taylor hadn’t been fined prior to Week 8, but plenty of his teammates had: Week 1: Calvin Ridley, unnecessary roughness, striking/kicking/tripping/kneeing, $12,537 Week 2: Calvin Ridley, unnecessary roughness, striking/kicking/tripping/kneeing, $12,537 Week 2: Jeffery Simmons, unnecessary roughness, $11,941 Week 4: John Franklin-Myers, unnecessary roughness, striking/kicking/tripping/kneeing, $12,537 Week 5: Micah Robinson, unnecessary roughness, hip-drop tackle, $5,583 The NFL splits the funds it collects from player fines between the NFLPA’s initiatives to support retired players and the NFL Foundation and other organizations that support youth football programs, player safety initiatives, and community health efforts.

title: NFL fined three Commanders defenders for actions in Eagles win
summary: The NFL has fined Commanders defensive lineman Charles Omenihu and edge rushers Odafe Oweh and K’Lavon Chaisson for infractions stemming from Washington’s victory over the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 8. Omenihu was fined $14,926 for unsportsmanlike conduct, with the league citing a violent gesture the issue, with 6 minutes, 20 seconds left in the third […]
full_text: The NFL has fined Commanders defensive lineman Charles Omenihu and edge rushers Odafe Oweh and K’Lavon Chaisson for infractions stemming from Washington’s victory over the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 8. Omenihu was fined $14,926 for unsportsmanlike conduct, with the league citing a violent gesture the issue, with 6 minutes, 20 seconds left in the third quarter. Oweh was fined $17,911 for a hit on quarterback Tanner McKee using his body weight with 31 seconds left in the game. Chaisson was also fined for a hit on McKee, with a blow to the head and neck, with 10 seconds left in the third quarter. The NFL announces that information on Saturdays. Whether fans agree with the calls or not, the NFL continues to protect quarterbacks (and its brand) and defensive players often take the brunt of the punishment for it while making split-second decisions in the heat of the moment. What do you think of these fines levied by the NFL on Washington’s players? Let us know in the comments below:

full_text: UPDATE: The Commanders made the Jer’Zhan Newton activation from injured reserve on Saturday afternoon, formally making him available for Sunday’s game against the L.A. Rams. That move was expected after he practiced in full all week leading up to this game. We have made the following roster moves: – Activated DT Jer’Zhan Newton from the Reserve/Injured List and removed him from the injury report – Placed WR Dyami Brown on the Reserve/Injured List – Elevated WR Jaden Bradley from the practice squad pic.twitter.com/oPVlyqq9Jj — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) November 7, 2026 As you can see in the Commanders’ tweet above, that wasn’t the only IR move of the day. Backup receiver Dyami Brown was placed on injured reserve after suffering a calf injury during Thursday’s practice. Head coach Dan Quinn said on Friday that the injury was concerning. He won’t be eligible to return until Week 13. Jaden Bradley was a practice-squad elevation for Sunday’s game, with fellow receiver Treylon Burks already ruled out with a foot injury. The Commanders have five receivers on the active roster — Van Jefferson was added earlier this week — and could manage with that number. The Washington Commanders are expected to announce a few roster moves before they host the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday afternoon. One move has already been reported, DT Jer’Zhan Newton (pec) is expected to be activated from injured reserve. His 21-day practice window was opened last week, but he didnt get activated to play vs the Eagles. He rejoins a team that just lost both their starting defensive tackles to season-ending injuries that required surgery this week. Newton was a full participant in practice this week and should make his return on Sunday. The #Commanders are activating DL Johnny Newton, who practiced fully all week as he's recovering from a torn pectoral muscle, to the 53-man roster from IR. He was previously listed as questionable. pic.twitter.com/FCJVm4iVRq — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) November 7, 2026 The Commanders released their injury report on Friday and ruled out WRs Treylon Burks (foot) and Dyami Brown (calf). title: Five Washington Commanders players key to beating Rams in NFL Week 9
summary: The Commanders are looking for their first winning streak of 2026. They’ve only won two games thus far but they weren’t earned in a row. While Washington simply must start stacking wins, they’ve been competitive while working towards playing four good quarters of football.   That will be a requirement to beat an L.A. Rams […]
full_text: The Commanders are looking for their first winning streak of 2026. They’ve only won two games thus far but they weren’t earned in a row. While Washington simply must start stacking wins, they’ve been competitive while working towards playing four good quarters of football. That will be a requirement to beat an L.A. Rams team with a so-so record but tons of star power, including quarterback Matt Stafford and defensive linemen Aaron Donald and Myles Garrett. All those dudes wear gold jackets someday. They Rams are also missing some key players, including Davonte Adams and Jaylen Warren on injured reserve. The Commanders IR list is also a who’s who, with Daron Payne, Laremy Tunsil, Terry McLaurin and Javon Kinlaw unavailable now and for the long-term. The Commanders will need important role players to step up and play huge in this one. Quarterback Jayden Daniels is the biggest and most obvious star on the team, so we’ll leave him off this list, but we’ll detial five more players to watch in Sunday’s key NFC matchup at Northwest Stadium. WR Stefon Diggs Dan Quinn was frank about the Commanders giving Antonio Williams more opportunities with Terry McLaurin done for the season. That was no smokescreen. The third-round rookie led the team with seven targets during Week 8. He’s playing but remains someone new to the pro game. But Stefon Diggs is the real No. 1 around here now. He has five touchdowns, though his 61.4% catch rate is the lowest of his career (just barely). While catch rate isn’t exclusively a receiver stat, he and Jayden Daniels must find greater connection. Look, he won’t be the dominant player of a few years back and the Commanders will spread the ball around, but Diggs’ leadership has been excellent. Now, his production needs an uptick starting on Sunday. EDGE K’Lavon Chaisson K’Lavon Chaisson has been Washington’s best edge defender this season, leading the team in overall pressures while producing against the run and pass. This is a game where quick pressures are essential and the Commanders might not blitz as much as expected considering Rams quarterback Matt Stafford’s ability to beat it. Odafe Oweh could’ve easily made this list, but the Commanders need an impact from both sides of the defensive front. DL Johnny Newton This is a bit of a speculative inclusion because Johnny Newton is reportedly getting activated , but hasn’t been formally activated off injured reserve as of the time of this story’s publication. He has practiced for two weeks and was a full participant this week, heading into Week 9. Washington needs him after seeing Javon Kinlaw and Daron Payne land on season-ending injured reserve. Newton joined the Commanders with high expectations as a 2024 second-round NFL draft pick . He hasn’t lived up to those expectatons thus far, though a torn pectoral muscle from this preseason certainly set that effort back. It’s always interesting to see how much a player returning off injured reserve can provide in terms of snap volume, but snap quality must be there. Stafford is a true pocket passer, and the fastest way to disrupt those guys is through interior pressure, forcing a quick throw, flushing him from the pocket, or a getting to him for a sack. The Commanders defensive line was good last week against Philadelphia, especially Charles Omenihu and Shy Tuttle. Adding some juice on critical downs especially could be beneficial to a team that’ll need some game-changing plays. TE John Bates It may seem like an odd choice to include someone with just five catches for 27 yards this season, but hear us out. The Rams have some heft off the edge, especially with Myles Garrett’s return off injured reserve. That man’s the best edge rusher on the planet and will require extra attention. At times, it’s a tight end one-on-one. That’s never a good matchup for anyone. Bates is one of the better blocking tight ends around – he was dealing with a shoulder injury this week but didn’t receive a designation — and could be an important part of the pass protection. We could throw the Commanders running backs into this effort, especially with Aaron Donald working from the inside. Washington lost its best pass protecting back in Jeremy McNichols, but Rachaad White and Austin Ekeler must hold it down as the last line of Jayden Daniels’ protection. S Nick Cross Defensive coordinator Daronte Jones loves moving Nick Cross around his alignment . He’s a blitzer, an active run defender in the box, a slot cornerback, and a deep safety. Cross is impactful in most every area, and has been a vital asset since returning from an illness that caused hospitalization in Week 2. The Commanders need to attack the ball, set up third-and-unmanageable, and then win on critical downs. Having a versatile defensive back that is an unpredictable, roving chess piece should help those efforts. Who else would you include in your list of Commanders to watch during Sunday’s game against L.A.? Let us know in the comments below.

title: Commanders win-loss projections for next 5 games – survey results
summary: Looking one month into the past A month ago, at the beginning of October, Washington had a record of 1-3, and things were looking decidedly grim for a team that had just lost both its starting and backup quarterbacks — and then lost to an inferior Colts team in London with Commanders rookie Athan Kaliakmanis, […]
full_text: Looking one month into the past A month ago, at the beginning of October, Washington had a record of 1-3, and things were looking decidedly grim for a team that had just lost both its starting and backup quarterbacks — and then lost to an inferior Colts team in London with Commanders rookie Athan Kaliakmanis, formerly of Rutgers, being pressed into service when Marcus Mariota was knocked out of the game in the first quarter. Dark times, indeed. Back then, as the Commanders headed into mid-October, we asked Hogs Haven members to predict, in the Reacts survey , how many wins Washington would rack up in the 3 games scheduled in the then-upcoming month, which would see the burgundy & gold go against the Giants and Eagles at home, as well as the 49ers on the road, with a bye week thrown in to boot. It’s interesting to look back on the results of that October survey in which about 1/3 of respondents predicted a 1-2 record; another 1/3 predicted a 2-1 record, and over a quarter of respondents predicted that Washington would get completely shut out, going 0-3. The predicted number of wins in that poll, calculated as a mathematical average, was 1.17. As we all know, the team actually ended up going 1-1-1, approximating the predicted number of wins in our survey, and out-performing the number of wins projected by 62% of respondents in that October survey. Fast forward to the present As dismal as the season may seem at the moment, if you can cast your mind back to that time early October — when fans were unsure who was going to take snaps at quarterback in Week 5 against the Giants, and nearly 30% of the fan base was expecting an 0-3 record for the upcoming month — you may come to the same conclusion that I have; that is, that the actual on-field results have improved (.250 in the first 4 weeks; .500 in the next 4 weeks), and the outlook for the 2026 season appears a little bit brighter than it did back then. After all, Jayden Daniels has started and finished 3 complete games since that survey was conducted. And, in the 6 quarters of football played since halftime at San Francisco in Week 6, the Commanders were highly competitive vs the 49ers, outscoring them 14-3 to make a game out of that prime time contest, and they actually beat the Eagles 27-10 this past Sunday. Sure, a lot of fans and media personalities are calling for Dan Quinn’s head one-third of the way through Season 3 of the rebuild recalibration, but the team still has every opportunity to meet or exceed preseason expectations by finishing strong, compiling 8 or 9 wins, and — given the current state of the NFC East — potentially winning the division and earning a home playoff game. While that still seems like a big ask with the team having just 2 wins in November, Hogs Haven readers who completed the Reacts survey this week seem to think that the Commanders can win more games than they lose over the next 5 weeks, and that — with respect to winning the division — no game will be more important than the road trip to New York five days from now to play the Giants. The upcoming five weeks — and especially Thursday’s Week 10 prime time game against the Giants — are critical to the Commanders 2026 season, and have the capacity, if Washington can beat New York and at least 2 other opponents in that slate of games, to set the team up for an exciting stretch run in the final weeks of the season. This Week’s Reacts Survey In this week’s Hogs Haven Reacts survey , we asked readers two questions to measure community sentiment entering the ninth week of the season. The first question was our weekly staple, asking whether you are confident in the overall direction of the team. This week, 43% of respondents answered “Yes,” while 57% voted “No.” The 21-point jump from last week’s mark was predictable; nothing lifts the collective mood around Washington quite like beating the Philadelphia Eagles. After struggling through a mistake-filled first quarter on Sunday night, Washington played nearly three full quarters of (fairly) disciplined, competitive football to overcome the early 10-point deficit and put away a division rival in a game that was critical to any hope the Commanders have of reaching the playoffs in 2026. Of course, a 57% negative vote is still a clear reminder of the frustration built up from a rocky first two months, but putting an NFC East win in the bank goes some way toward soothing the unease of the fanbase. Looking at November (and a little beyond) Our second question turned the focus forward: What record will the Commanders compile in the next 5 games? The upcoming slate features the Los Angeles Rams (4-4) at home before a quick turnaround trip to New York to take on the division-leading Giants (4-2-1) on Thursday Night Football. There is a mini-bye of sorts ahead of a home date against the Cincinnati Bengals (5-2) on Monday Night Football, which is followed by road trips to play the Arizona Cardinals (3-5) and Tennessee Titans (1-7). Sizing Up the Next Five Games When the votes were tallied for this second survey question, 10% of respondents had predicted a 5-0 sweep; 25% predicted 4 wins; 39% projected 3 wins; 17% expected 2 wins; 8% voted for 1 win, and just 1% foresaw a 0-5 collapse. Visit our partners at FanDuel My takeaway from those numbers is that nearly three-quarters of our community—74% of respondents, to be exact—expect Washington to put together a winning record over this upcoming five-game stretch. The single largest group, representing a 39% plurality, landed squarely on a 3-2 outcome. Only about a quarter of Hogs Haven voters anticipate a losing record over this stretch, and just 9% foresee complete disaster with fewer than two victories. That represents a dramatic shift in tone from where things stood just a few weeks ago. Mathematically, Hogs Haven readers responding to this week’s survey projected an average win total of 3.09 — strongly suggesting that our in-house prognosticators, who projected the win total so closely last time around, have a strong collective belief that the Commanders will go 3-2 in the coming five weeks, putting together the first multi-game stretch of the season above .500. When you consider the sheer amount of deep concern that accompanied the team’s sluggish start, seeing roughly three out of every four voters project winning football between now and early December shows that most of the fan base still believes this roster has life in it – at least enough life to get some wins against the relatively lightweight set of opponents that Washington will face in the next several weeks. What a winning record in the next 5 games would mean The strategic significance of that projected 3-2 run is notable. If the Commanders manage to win three of the next five, they would enter Week 14 with a 5-6-1 record. With five games left on the schedule at that juncture, an 8-win or 9-win season would morph from an offseason daydream into an attainable mathematical reality. In a division that has shown plenty of vulnerability from top to bottom, being within striking distance of a .500 record by early-to-mid-December should keep Washington in position to compete for the NFC East division title. Alex Rowsey said it in as many words in the comments: “In this division, if they win 3 of those games (with 1 coming against NYG), they’ll be sitting in pretty good shape at 5-6-1 after Week 13.” Playoffs?? Playoffs??!! The thought process behind the projection of 3 victories doesn’t seem too mysterious. Most survey respondents who forecast a winning stretch seem to view the road games against the Cardinals and the Titans as ones in which Washington should be able to take care of business. Arizona has struggled to string together consistent four-quarter efforts, having logged wins over the Rams, Cowboys, and winless Chargers (3 teams with a combined 7-16 record), while Tennessee sits at 1-7, their lone victory coming in Week 6 against the lowly Indianapolis Colts (yes, I remember…

title: Week 9 betting preview: Analysis, best bets, TD predictions for Sunday
summary: Our experts dive into the odds and player props for Week 9 and offer their betting tips and favorite plays.
full_text:
Value is value, no matter where -- or how -- you find it. And that's what we'll aim to do each week in this space: Find betting value.

 Ben Solak, Seth Walder and Matt Bowen bring different perspectives into how they approach sports betting. Solak leans on his expertise in player evaluation and the X's and O's to find edges, while Walder relies on statistical models to pick out plus-expected value bets, focusing mainly on defense. Bowen, a former NFL safety, predicts positive matchups and game winners from tape study and his understanding of the league. Also included are fantasy projection creator Mike Clay's top predicted anytime TD scorers for Week 9.

 From spreads and money lines to totals and defensive player props, a good price might be found anywhere. Results will be tracked throughout the season, with flat one-unit wagers for each listed bet. Let's get into it.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 Jump to: 
 Bowen's favorite bets 
 Solak's plays  | Walder's props 
 Clay's TD projections 

 

 

 Bowen's favorite bets 
 Heading into the Week 9 Sunday slate, I'm going to start with the late-window Packers-Patriots matchup in New England, giving you my pick for the game. I have some thoughts there on the Green Bay defense based on what it is showing on the tape. Plus, I have a couple more game picks to look at -- including a two-team teaser -- and I'll throw down some props, too.

 Green Bay Packers  at New England Patriots 
4:25 p.m. ET on Fox; Line: NE -3.5, O/U: 45.5

 

 I'll start with the Packers' defense under coordinator Jonathan Gannon. This unit is playing its best football of the season, allowing 14.8 PPG over the past four while giving up just 4.5 yards per play. The Packers are taking the ball away, too, recording 11 turnovers in this four-game stretch. We'll see a lot of late movement in the secondary, with multiple fronts and disguised pressures, which will force Patriots quarterback Drake Maye to read it out post-snap with a wide receiver group that is still banged up. Offensively for the Packers, the combo of Christian Watson and Matthew Golden creates vertical opportunities for quarterback Jordan Love . My concern here? Can Green Bay get the running game going with Josh Jacobs ? I don't see a burst yet from Jacobs, which the Packers will need to attack the edges on outside zone run concepts. But with the added prep time, I like Green Bay to cover here .

 Denver Broncos -2.5 at Carolina Panthers 

 

 The Panthers' offensive line is beat up, and they can't protect consistently on the edges, as quarterback Bryce Young has been sacked 11 times over the last two games. That's trouble versus a Denver pass rush that has a pressure rate of 40.4% (second highest in the league). Yes, Jonah Coleman can give the Broncos' run game a boost versus a Panthers defense allowing 140.7 rushing yards per game (third most), but I'm taking Denver because of its ability to disrupt the pocket.

 Two team, 6.5-point teaser (-143): Arizona Cardinals +15 at Seattle Seahawks , Detroit Lions -0.5 at Miami Dolphins 

 Moving the Cardinals to +15 points at Seattle, which will have Drew Lock making the start for an injured Sam Darnold , feels more comfortable. I like this Cardinals offense with Gardner Minshew II at quarterback, too. Minshew is fearless with the ball. And while that can lead to turnover situations, Minshew has the movement traits to keep plays alive, which will allow Arizona to compete at a higher rate on Sunday.

 Teasing the Lions down to almost a moneyline play is the smart move here on the road in Miami. Detroit showed us last week that it can go run-heavy with Jahmyr Gibbs to close out games, and we know the Lions will have pass-game answers for a Miami defense that has been more zone-heavy this season.

 
 Check out the latest Super Bowl odds and major NFL awards futures . 

 

 Jahmyr Gibbs receiving yards OVER 26.5 (-116) 

 I missed on Gibbs last week, but this is a good matchup for him in the passing game. Miami is allowing 40.6 receiving yards per game to opposing running backs, and Gibbs has 27 or more yards in six of seven games played this season.

 Bryce Young passing yards UNDER 237.5 passing yards (-113) 

 I rarely play the under, but Young has thrown for fewer than 210 yards in each of his past two starts. And as we discussed above, the Broncos' pass rush has matchup advantages here on the edges.

 Blake Corum rushing yards OVER 49.5 (-112) 

 Corum has seen his usage jump over the past two weeks, rushing for at least 73 yards -- with 11 or more carries -- in back-to-back games. With a Sunday matchup versus a Washington defense that is now down defensive linemen Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw due to season-ending injuries, I like Corum to hit the over.

 Malachi Fields anytime TD (+475) 

 Let's take a shot here on Fields at Philly. The rookie caught his only touchdown pass of the season back in Week 4, but he has the physical tools to win boundary matchups. And in Week 7 with J.J. McCarthy making the start for the Giants, Fields caught four of five targets (with one end zone target) for 83 yards.

 Joe Burrow - Michael Penix Jr . combined pass yards 500+ (-112) 

 Let's try something new here with Burrow and Penix throwing for a combined total of 500 or more yards. Both defenses in this matchup rank in the bottom 15 in passing yards allowed, and Burrow has thrown for more than 420 yards in two of his past four starts. Penix? Throw out the weather game last week. He has posted 220-plus passing yards in four of six starts this season.

 

 

 
 Solak's plays 

 

 Atlanta Falcons +3 (-102) vs. Cincinnati Bengals 

 I really like this matchup for the Falcons -- always a scary thing to say after a team scored zero points and lost to an opponent who completed zero passes. But I do! The Falcons have a 40% pressure rate, the sixth-highest number in football, and they're facing a Bengals team that is passing the football more than any other team in the league. They're going to be able to accumulate hits on Joe Burrow , and they're going to get some stops in the air, too. Per Next Gen Stats, the Falcons are tight to routes downfield, only allowing 2.0 yards of separation on throws of at least 10 air yards and forcing a tight window on 34.8% of those pass attempts. Both of those numbers are second best in the league. The Falcons just had to play a deep run of teams with healthy rushing attacks (the 49ers, Bears, Buccaneers, Ravens). When they've played unbalanced teams like the Packers or Saints, this defense has really shined.

 Offensively, the Falcons catch Cincinnati at a good moment, as star Bengals cornerback  DJ Turner II  is dealing with a heel injury. He returned to practice Thursday, but his status for Sunday morning in Madrid is uncertain. Look for Drake London to have a big contest on the outside, and the Bengals have always had issues handling tight ends, so Kyle Pitts Sr . could see increased volume as well. This is a great stylistic fight for a Falcons team desperate to stay in the NFC South race. I love them to cover the spread.

 Christian Watson receptions UNDER 4.5 (+105) 

 

 It's a tough draw Sunday for Watson, who will see the combination of Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis III on the outside in New England. The Patriots are also a heavy man-cover team, running it at the third-highest rate in football, and Watson has been less productive against man coverage this year than in seasons past when he was the only shot-play specialist on the roster. With Matthew Golden 's emergence, Watson is no longer the team leader in targets per route run versus man coverage (27.0% to 30.1%).

 My expectation for this matchup is that Patriots DC Zak Kuhr will blitz heavily and try to force Jordan Love into even quicker throws than normal (Love gets rid of the ball at the quickest rate in the league). title: 2026 NFL trade deadline: Proposing deals for Tony Pollard, Riq Woolen, others
summary: Our NFL experts pitched trade offers they'd love to see get done before Tuesday's deadline, including moves for Tony Pollard, Riq Woolen, Jonathan Taylor and Jessie Bates III.
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline is three days away, and we've already seen a handful of major moves from teams. The Colts traded away cornerstones on both sides of the ball, with guard Quenton Nelson  to the Seahawks and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner  to the 49ers. And the Bears dealt a package that included two first-round picks to land Titans defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons . Two quarterbacks have also switched teams, with J.J. McCarthy going to the Giants and Jacoby Brissett joining the Ravens.

 But what other big deals could be on the horizon? Ahead of Tuesday's 4 p.m. ET deadline , we asked eight experts from ESPN and NFL Network to pitch realistic trade offers that they would love to see get done. They laid out the compensation for each team and then explained why the deals would make sense for both parties involved.

 Here are the trades they are proposing, starting with the running back on everyone's mind ahead of the deadline.

 

 
 Jump to a deal for a player: 
 Bates | Brown | Downs |  Ojomo 
 Pollard  |  Suamataia | Taylor | Woolen 

 
 

 Judy Battista's offer 
 

 Minnesota Vikings get: RB Jonathan Taylor 
 Indianapolis Colts get: 2027 second-round pick, 2027 third-round pick, 2027 fifth-round pick, 2027 fifth-round pick ( acquired from NYG )

 Why this deal makes sense for both sides: It's a haul (similar to one that sent RB  Christian McCaffrey  to the 49ers in 2022), but the Vikings need Taylor's home run threat to pair with QB  Kyler Murray 's explosive rushing ability. Up until this point of the season, their offense has been largely stagnant despite the presence of receivers Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison .

 The Vikings have arguably the best defense in the league, but they'll need to score points for a deep playoff run. The Colts, engaged in a fire sale and potentially  hoping to get a first-rounder for Taylor, get plenty of draft picks to help kickstart what looks like a total rebuild.

 

 
 

 Matt Bowen's offer 
 

 Chicago Bears get: CB Riq Woolen 
 Philadelphia Eagles get: 2027 fifth-round pick

 Why this deal makes sense for both sides: The Bears already made an aggressive trade for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons -- a game changer in the front -- but they still need more top-end speed in the back end. Woolen brings the physical traits and boundary speed to play man coverage with his 6-foot-4 frame, plus he fits in coordinator Dennis Allen's split-safety schemes as a ball disruptor (12 interceptions and 59 pass breakups in his career).

 For the Eagles, they get a Day 3 return on Woolen, who is set to be a free agent in 2027 after signing a one-year deal with Philly.

 

 
 Jeremy Fowler's offer 
 

 Kansas City Chiefs get: WR  Josh Downs 
 Indianapolis Colts get: 2027 fourth-round pick

 Why this deal makes sense for both sides: Kansas City has been looking for receiver help, and Indianapolis is weighing trade options for Downs, who wants out . The Colts would love a third-round pick for him but might need to settle for a fourth. The Chiefs would get a much-needed additional playmaker, and the Colts would strengthen their rebuild, though Downs' absence would badly hurt an already struggling offense.

 

 

 
 Aaron Schatz's offer 
 

 Los Angeles Rams get: WR Dyami Brown , 2027 seventh-round pick 
 Washington Commanders get: 2027 sixth-round pick

 Why this deal makes sense for both sides: Don't be fooled by Brown's low average of 10.4 yards per reception; he's primarily a deep threat who stretches the field. And though it feels like he has been around for years, he's still only 27 years old.

 For the Rams, Brown would probably be a better receiving option than Tutu Atwell . And more importantly for coach Sean McVay's offense, Brown is a better run blocker with 30 pounds on Atwell. Brown shouldn't demand much of a return, and the Rams don't have a 2027 seventh-round pick (it was flipped to the Ravens in 2024 as part of a deal involving CB  Tre'Davious White ).

 

 
 Ben Solak's offer 
 

 Green Bay Packers get: RB Tony Pollard 
 Tennessee Titans get: 2027 fourth-round pick

 Why this deal makes sense for both sides: Even if the Packers trust they'll have running back  Josh Jacobs for the rest of the season after his six-game stint on the commissioner exempt list , his lack of explosive runs is disqualifying from consistent 15-plus-carry games. Jacobs' longest run of the season is 10 yards, and he is 26th out of 35 running backs in 10-plus-yard rush rate since the start of last season. Meanwhile, Pollard is 11th and has the necessary pass-catching chops to play all three downs in Green Bay's offense.

 The Packers have an extra fourth-round pick, thanks to the Rashan Gary trade with Dallas in March, and could easily flip it to introduce more balance to their playoff-contending team.

 

 
 Seth Walder's offer 
 

 Buffalo Bills get: S Jessie Bates III 
 Atlanta Falcons get: 2027 third-round pick, 2028 sixth-round pick

 Note: Atlanta would convert all but the minimum of Bates' remaining 2026 base salary into a signing bonus prior to this proposed trade. 

 Why this deal makes sense for both sides: The  release of C.J. Gardner-Johnson means there is a perfect opening for Bates -- one of the game's best safeties -- in Buffalo's secondary. But the sneaky reason why this could happen? The Falcons have over $109 million of 2027 cap space (most in the NFL), per OverTheCap.com. So they're almost guaranteed to be active in free agency, which in turn means there's a chance they wouldn't get a compensatory pick for Bates (because signings cancel out departures when compensatory picks are distributed). If the Falcons keep Bates through the deadline, the risk they lose him for nothing is high.

 Buffalo is in the opposite cap situation, so this would be like a short-term signing. But Bates probably would net them something like a fourth-round compensatory pick in 2028 if he signed elsewhere next offseason, significantly softening how much draft capital Buffalo is giving up in this scenario.

 

 
 Cameron Wolfe's offer 
 

 Jacksonville Jaguars get: DT Moro Ojomo 
 Philadelphia Eagles get: 2027 third-round pick, 2028 fourth-round pick

 Why this deal makes sense for both sides: The Jaguars were already looking heavy into interior defensive line upgrades before their elite run-stopping nose tackle  DaVon Hamilton  suffered a season-ending quad injury Sunday. Now an addition feels mandatory for this Super Bowl-contending team. Ojomo looks like the best option available, and he would be an excellent fit as a three-down disruptor next to Arik Armstead .

 At times, Ojomo has looked like the Eagles' best defensive lineman on tape this season. And though they value him a lot, he is a free agent after this season on a team that already granted big deals to DTs  Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis . This move would allow the 2-6 Eagles to load up on more draft capital, locking in two middle-round picks instead of one potential compensatory pick if Ojomo left in free agency.

 

 
 
 

 Field Yates' offer 
 

 Green Bay Packers get: OL Kingsley Suamataia 
 Kansas City Chiefs get: 2027 fourth-round pick

 Why this deal makes sense for both sides:  After starting all of last season for the Chiefs, Suamataia has been benched twice this season  despite backup options yielding less than optimal results in his stead. However, he could still be a valuable asset to another team given he's just 23, has positional versatility and is under contract through next season. The Packers must continue to hurl resources at an offensive line that has battled injuries and ineffectiveness through eight weeks, so giving up a fourth-round pick is worth it.

title: Bengals face Falcons S Jessie Bates III, evoking mixed emotions
summary: Cincinnati hasn't been to the playoffs since Bates' departure, but Atlanta also hasn't reached the postseason since his arrival.
full_text:
MADRID -- When the Cincinnati Bengals step on the field at the Santiago Bernabeu in Madrid on Sunday to face the Atlanta Falcons , the Bengals will be posed with a question it once forced other teams to ask.

 How does one account for safety Jessie Bates III ? 

 From 2018 to 2022, Bates emerged as one of Cincinnati's best playmakers in the team's run to the Super Bowl at the end of the 2021 season. But after Bates left Cincinnati in free agency, he has spent the past four seasons with the Falcons, with whom he has maintained his perch as one of the best in the NFL.

 And ahead of Sunday's game, Bates was asked how much he thinks about the events that led him to leave the team that drafted him.

 "Coming here to Atlanta has changed my life, my family's trajectory, what that looks like moving forward," Bates told ESPN. "But at the same time, it's like, damn, you want to play in meaningful football games. I haven't played in the playoffs since I left there. And I don't think they've been in the playoffs, either, since I left."

 Bates is correct. The Falcons (3-5) could use a win to jump-start their season and break a nine-year postseason drought. Cincinnati (5-2) is looking to secure its first playoff berth since 2022.

 That was Bates' last season with Cincinnati, which drafted him in 2018 with a second-round pick. Bengals coach Zac Taylor, who arrived a year after Bates was drafted, recalled how the former Wake Forest standout went from a young player adjusting to a new scheme to an ascending star.

 "He was really just a perfect example of a guy that just shows growth from every year, from years one through five, and proud of the way he attacked it," said Taylor, who continued to extoll everything from Bates' reputation in the locker room and community to how he received coaching. "I don't usually spend this much time praising the other team, but Jessie's one that I've always really liked."

 But that growth clashed with a couple of the NFL's realities. In a league with a salary cap, decisions must be made on which players are considered most essential. And after quarterback Joe Burrow and the passing attack proved to be one of the best in the NFL, that's what the Bengals spent their resources on.

 In hindsight, even just looking at the financial aspect of the decision, one could argue it cost the Bengals more to let Bates leave.

 Bates signed with the Falcons on a four-year deal worth just over $64 million. The contract included guaranteed money in the second year, which is something Cincinnati only just started doing for non-quarterbacks.

 Since then, Cincinnati has tried four players in Bates' former role. The combined value of those contracts is $77.9 million, according to OverTheCap.com. That includes the rookie deal for current Bengals cornerback Dax Hill , a 2022 first-round pick who has never settled into a full-time position after initially being drafted to replace Bates.

 This offseason, the Bengals took their biggest swing at correcting the decision. They signed former  Bryan Cook , who was on two Super Bowl-winning teams with the Chiefs, to a three-year deal worth just over $40 million.

 And though the secondary has still had its ups and downs, defensive coordinator Al Golden has been very pleased with how the team's current safeties stack up.

 " Jordan [Battle ] can stand on his own," Golden said. "Obviously, [ Kyle] Dugger  has been in the league seven years. He can stand on his own. Cook has solidified himself in this league and is a champion."

 Though Atlanta hasn't been successful as a club, the 29-year-old Bates has racked up career accolades. He reached the Pro Bowl in 2023, his first year with the Falcons, and is a two-time second-team All-Pro selection.

 This season, he has been just as dynamic. According to ESPN Research, Bates and the New York Giants' Jevon Holland are the only safeties with multiple forced fumbles, an interception and at least four pass deflections.

 And the impact goes beyond the numbers. Falcons defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich said Bates was one of the best players he had ever been around in nearly three decades in the NFL.

 "As long as you've got Jessie Bates on your defense, you've got a chance because he's going to make sure he's going to touch every single human being from the front to the back and make sure we get the best version of them," Ulbrich said.

 On Sunday, it will be the Bengals' turn to account for Bates. On Thursday in Madrid, he said it will be exciting and bittersweet to go up against players he knows well and a franchise that produced "some of the best times of my life."

 And it will be a reminder of just how things can go in the NFL.

 "That's just part of the business," Bates said. "Sometimes, you got to leave a spot that you love, and there's more blessings on the other side of it."

title: Inside the evolution of Caleb Williams' MVP candidacy
summary: Williams has the fourth-shortest odds to win MVP as the Bears are currently favored to win the NFC.
full_text:
Chicago Bears  wide receiver  Luther Burden III ran back to the visitors sideline at Seattle's Lumen Field on Monday night with a message for quarterback Caleb Williams .

 The Bears had just accomplished a rare feat. Before Burden caught a 1-yard touchdown pass at the end of an opening drive that spanned 8 minutes, 32 seconds, the last team to score a touchdown against Seattle on its first possession was the 49ers in Week 1 of the 2025 season.

 "I went up to him and told him I don't care who they is," the wide receiver said about the defending Super Bowl champs. "No. 1 defense, I don't care."

 After slapping hands with his teammate, Williams stood up from the bench and echoed Burden's sentiment.

 "I don't give a f--- who they are!" Williams yelled.

 Chicago's 34-17 takedown of the Seahawks capped a unique set of primetime performances as the Bears beat Super Bowl runner-up New England in Week 7 and the defending champs in back-to-back games. It was the first such sequence in franchise history.

 

 The victory made the Bears the favorites to represent the NFC in Super Bowl LXI, and it planted Williams firmly in the MVP conversation. Williams entered Week 9 with the fourth-shortest odds (+500) to win MVP, according to DraftKings Sportsbook. He trailed the Buffalo Bills' Josh Allen (+165), San Francisco 49ers' Brock Purdy (+450) and Cincinnati Bengals' Joe Burrow (+475).

 The Bears (6-2) have won all three games since Williams returned from a hamstring injury that sidelined him Weeks 3-5. In fact, they haven't trailed in any of the three and have topped 30 points each time. That streak will be challenged Sunday night by a visiting Tampa Bay Buccaneers team yielding just 18.9 points per game, the fifth-best mark in the league.

 Then again, no quarterback had thrown for 200 yards on Seattle's defense in 2026 until Williams reached 247. That was his third game with at least one touchdown, no interceptions and a 70% or higher completion percentage this season, tying him for the league lead, according to ESPN Research.

 Williams ranks second in completion percentage (70.9%), fourth in interception rate (0.6), seventh in success rate (51.1), fifth in yards per attempt (8.0) and 11th in yards per game (253.4). He is third in QBR (78.9), third in EPA per dropback (0.24) and fifth in win probability added (117.0%).

 Here's a look at how Williams has played his way into the MVP mix.

 Why Caleb Williams' decisiveness wins 
 One of the last things Williams and USC coach Lincoln Riley would utter during Trojans quarterback meetings was to be decisive.

 "When you're hesitant, bad things happen," Williams said. "So, decisiveness wins is what I go by, a slogan I go by."

 While he was sidelined for three games, Williams often thought about ways he could demonstrate better decisiveness when he got back on the field. The things that would allow him to play faster and deliver a cleaner ball to his intended target meant having conviction in where his reads would take him.

 "Most of the time, you're seeing less of the superhero plays," backup quarterback Tyson Bagent said. "He's only letting that come when it presents itself.

 

 "Other than that, he's anticipating things like I haven't seen him do before, and he's just in a good rhythm, playing at a high level."

 That decisiveness has generated more consistency in the passing game. Williams became the first Bears quarterback since Mitchell Trubisky in 2018 to throw for 300 yards in back-to-back wins over the Falcons and Patriots.

 It has also elevated the play of his top pass catchers. After totaling 13 receptions for 110 yards in the first five games of the season, tight end Colston Loveland has turned 20 catches into 199 yards and two touchdowns since Williams' return in Week 6.

 Williams' decisiveness has allowed him to become the NFL's most successful quarterback when not under duress. He has completed 86% of his passes (96 of 112 attempts) when not pressured, the highest completion percentage when not pressured by any quarterback through five starts of a season since ESPN began tracking pressures in 2009.

 And most impressively, he has yet to throw an interception on those 112 attempts.

 That's considerable improvement from last season, when he completed 66.2% of his passes without pressure, the third-lowest rate in the league along with the fourth-highest off-target rate (16.1%).

 In his past three games, Williams is 63-of-70 (90%) when not pressured. He leads all quarterbacks with an 85.7% completion rate when not under duress.

 Less Superman, more checkdowns are not a bad thing 
 One hallmark of Bears training camp practices was long-drive drills as the offense ate up the clock while deliberately moving the ball downfield.

 Those grind-it-out periods translated to the regular season. In total, the Bears have run 21 drives that went 10-plus plays (second most in the NFL), with 15 of those drives culminating in a touchdown or field goal.

 On the Bears' opening drive in Seattle, Williams led his unit 80 yards on 17 plays while attempting 10 short throws, none that resulted in more than a 15-yard completion.

 "I would say I've grown in that area," Williams said. "I can go back to high school; all I did was take shots. I went to college and scrambled around a little bit. I took a few checkdowns, very little.

 

 "And then my first year [in the NFL] was very little. I got sacked a lot, all that. Then this past year, I found a few more [checkdowns], scrambled still a little bit. And then this year, it's just being a lot more comfortable with the playbook and understanding it and what we want to do with certain plays. From there, being able to, when they don't get the specific coverage, just being able to check the ball down and keep the drive alive."

 That mindset is the catalyst behind Williams' 71% completion percentage, which ranks second behind Burrow. Williams ranks fifth in the NFL in yards per attempt (8.0) and 28th in air yards per attempt (6.5)

 The Bears' quarterback already has three games during which he has completed at least 70% of his passes after having none in 2025.

 "He's hitting the top of the drop and the ball's coming out where it's supposed to be or he's quickly down to a progression or checkdown to keep us on schedule," offensive coordinator Press Taylor said. "I think he and a lot of our guys realize now if we can in these normal-down situations, we're just going to keep unloading the clip, and we're going to keep firing and keep doing all this. When it's there, take it; when it's not, put it in play."

 Putting more on Caleb Williams' plate 
 In preparation for the reigning Super Bowl champion defense, Ben Johnson and his coaches created a game plan to combat the variety of fronts and pressures Seattle runs out of the same personnel groupings.

 The goal was to generate explosive runs while simultaneously reducing negative plays. It was a complex plan that demanded more from Williams to put the offense in position to succeed.

 "There were probably more kills on each and every run play than we normally have," Taylor said. "So, he's got a lot of responsibility in terms of diagnosing what the front is, understanding why we're killing a play or why we're changing a play based on what the look is, because they're not all the same."

 Williams battled through the stress that came with mastering this heavy pre-snap mental load. Taylor noted how frustrated the quarterback grew with himself in walk-throughs while spitting out the calls, well before this task got harder with the element of Seattle's crowd noise.

 By game time, the hiccups Williams had experienced were in the past.

 

 "He has so much going on," right tackle Darnell Wright said. "He'll start the week, he'll have all of his stuff and then by the time we get to the game, I don't know how -- he's obviously studying -- but for some reason, it starts off pretty bumpy. We all have our little bumps and then by the…
